title: HATM — Human and AI Trust Compatibility Module
text: HATM — Human and AI Trust Compatibility Module Parent Standard: Trust Layer Standard Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Human and AI Trust Compatibility Type: Trust Architecture Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 10 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Trust Layer Standard · Truth Validation Layer · Integrity Standard · Universal Canonical Language · Origin-Bound Identity · Audit in Real Time · AI Runtime Integrity Vault Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Human and AI Trust Compatibility Module defines the structural conditions under which trust may remain compatible, understandable, and continuously verifiable across both human interpretation and AI-executed operational logic. A system satisfies HATM only if: trust conditions remain readable for humans and machine-operable for AI systems trust does not depend on human-only assumptions or machine-only logic meaning remains stable across human and AI interpretation operational trust can be verified without contradiction between human judgment and machine execution trust compatibility remains structurally preserved across hybrid environments A system that appears trustworthy to humans but cannot be operationally validated by AI, or appears valid to AI while remaining unintelligible or misleading to humans, does not satisfy HATM. Module Function HATM defines the compatibility layer of trust architecture between human and machine-governed environments. It ensures that trust is not split into two disconnected realities: one for human interpretation one for machine execution The module applies wherever trust must remain stable across: human oversight AI-supported systems autonomous execution hybrid operational environments cross-system interpretation machine-readable governance human-facing validation conditions Its function is to preserve one structurally compatible trust-state across both human and AI-operated environments. Step 1 — Define the Trust Compatibility Object The organization must define what trust relationship must remain compatible across humans and AI systems. Minimum requirement: the trust object is explicit the compatibility scope is bounded undefined compatibility targets are excluded from valid trust logic The trust object may include a: system process workflow AI agent operational decision path hybrid human-AI environment machine-assisted governance structure Step 2 — Define Human Trust Conditions The system must define what makes the trust-state understandable and valid from the human side. Minimum requirement: human trust conditions are explicit the trust-state is interpretable by accountable human actors trust does not depend on opaque machine output alone These conditions may include: understandable meaning accountable decision logic reviewable validation status visible responsibility structure non-deceptive interpretation boundaries Step 3 — Define AI Trust Conditions The system must define what makes the trust-state machine-readable and operationally valid from the AI side. Minimum requirement: AI trust conditions are explicit trust logic is interpretable under machine-operable structural rules trust does not depend on vague human intuition alone These conditions may include: canonical meaning consistency machine-readable validation logic runtime traceability structured integrity conditions bounded execution rules Step 4 — Define Compatibility Logic The system must define how human trust conditions and AI trust conditions remain aligned. Minimum requirement: compatibility logic is explicit contradiction between human-readable trust and machine-executed trust can be identified trust compatibility is not assumed merely because both humans and AI participate This means the system must ensure that: what humans believe they are trusting and what AI is actually executing under trust conditions remain structurally compatible. Step 5 — Define Meaning Stability Across Human and AI Interpretation The system must define how trust-related meaning remains stable across both human and machine interpretation. Minimum requirement: trust-related terms remain canonically consistent semantic drift between human reading and AI execution is restricted trust compatibility does not collapse through divergent interpretation of the same condition Without stable meaning, compatibility becomes symbolic rather than operational. Step 6 — Preserve Compatibility Traceability The system must preserve traceability of human and AI trust alignment. Minimum requirement: compatibility evidence is reviewable trust alignment remains auditable later reconstruction of trust compatibility remains possible If compatibility cannot be reconstructed, then trust across humans and AI becomes another unverified claim. Step 7 — Restrict Invalid Human and AI Trust Design The system must not be treated as valid if trust appears aligned only at the surface while structural incompatibility remains underneath. Minimum requirement: invalid trust compatibility conditions are identifiable symbolic alignment is excluded trust cannot be claimed as compatible if humans and AI operate under different effective trust logic Scenario A human supervisory team relies on an AI-supported system for operational decisions, but the machine interprets trust conditions differently from the human reviewers. Application HATM is used to ensure: trust conditions are explicit for both human and AI interpretation canonical meaning remains stable across both sides compatibility gaps between human oversight and machine execution can be identified trust does not appear aligned only because both sides use the same words differently Result The organization gains a stronger trust architecture in which human and AI trust conditions remain structurally compatible rather than only superficially similar. Scenario A hybrid environment combines human operators, automated systems, and AI execution layers across a shared workflow where trust must remain stable across all participants. Application HATM is used to ensure: trust remains readable for humans and executable for machines compatibility is preserved across interpretation and operation trust-state does not fragment between human assumptions and machine logic structural contradictions can be detected before operational failure occurs Result The environment gains a stronger basis for trust continuity because human and AI participation remain aligned within one compatible trust structure. Canonical Closing Statement If humans and AI cannot trust under the same structural conditions, trust becomes fragmented before the system fails. Related Documents → Trust Layer Standard (TLS™)

title: HCCM — Human Comfort Calibration Module
text: HCCM — Human Comfort Calibration Module Parent Standard: Continuous Interaction Layer Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Human Comfort Calibration Type: Continuous Interaction Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 12 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Continuous Interaction Layer · CLIA · RIS · OGL · EVIP · AIL · Autonomous Runtime Systems · Realtime AI Architectures Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English Canonical Definition Human Comfort Calibration Module defines the structural conditions under which a continuously present intelligent system remains behaviorally compatible with human comfort, interaction pacing, interruption tolerance, cognitive load boundaries, emotional timing, and socially acceptable realtime participation. A system satisfies HCCM only if: interaction pacing remains behaviorally appropriate interruption intensity remains bounded by human tolerance conditions continuous presence does not create avoidable discomfort, pressure, or overload proactive participation remains calibrated to human cognitive and social compatibility live interaction behavior remains governable not only technically, but experientially A system that remains continuously active while disregarding human comfort conditions does not satisfy HCCM. Module Function HCCM defines the human comfort layer of continuous interaction governance. It ensures that continuous interaction systems are not judged only by technical capability, low latency, or constant availability, but also by whether their live behavior remains tolerable, socially acceptable, and interaction-compatible for humans over time. The module applies wherever a system may continuously influence: conversational pacing interruption frequency attention pressure emotional timing live guidance intensity response persistence ambient presence comfort human cognitive load during ongoing interaction Its function is not to make a system merely pleasant. Its function is to prevent continuous participation from becoming behaviorally excessive, socially abrasive, cognitively draining, or experientially destabilizing. Step 1 — Define the Comfort Object The organization must define what aspect of human interaction comfort is being governed. Minimum requirement: the comfort object is explicit the scope of comfort calibration is structurally bounded undefined comfort targets are excluded from valid governance logic The comfort object may include: interruption behavior pacing rhythm response persistence timing of intervention cognitive intensity environmental presence behavior multimodal participation behavior interaction continuity over time Step 2 — Define Comfort-Relevant Interaction Conditions The system must define which interaction conditions are relevant to human comfort. Minimum requirement: comfort-relevant conditions are explicit the system does not reduce interaction quality to technical correctness alone behavioral influence on the human participant remains identifiable These conditions may include: interruption frequency timing sensitivity repetition intensity proactive intervention density speech pacing silence tolerance escalation pressure contextual emotional timing continuous presence burden Step 3 — Define Tolerance Boundaries The system must define the boundaries within which live participation remains behaviorally tolerable. Minimum requirement: tolerance boundaries are explicit behavior does not remain permanently active without calibration to human limits undefined behavioral intensity is excluded from valid comfort logic Tolerance boundaries may include limits of: interruption rate persistence of reminders urgency repetition attention capture intensity simultaneous information load response pressure escalation frequency presence duration without reset or relief Step 4 — Define Calibration Logic The system must define how interaction behavior is calibrated to preserve human comfort. Minimum requirement: calibration logic is explicit the system can distinguish acceptable intensity from excessive intensity behavioral adaptation does not occur through arbitrary or opaque logic alone This means the system must remain able to determine: when to speak when to wait when to interrupt when to reduce intensity when to maintain distance when to slow interaction pacing when to avoid unnecessary active presence Step 5 — Define Cognitive Load Protection The system must define how it avoids imposing unnecessary cognitive overload during continuous participation. Minimum requirement: cognitive load conditions are explicit the system does not treat continuous presence as permission for unlimited engagement overload risk remains governable This includes regulation of: information density multitasking pressure repeated prompting split-attention burden timing compression escalation during high-load conditions A continuously present system must remain aware not only of what it can do, but of what a human can comfortably sustain. Step 6 — Preserve Comfort Traceability The system must preserve traceability of comfort-relevant behavioral states and calibration changes. Minimum requirement: comfort-related behavior remains reviewable changes in pacing, interruption, and intensity remain reconstructable later audit can determine whether live behavior remained within governed comfort boundaries If human comfort effects cannot be reviewed, continuous interaction behavior becomes experientially opaque. Step 7 — Restrict Invalid Comfort Design The system must not be treated as valid if continuous presence remains technically effective but behaviorally excessive, socially abrasive, cognitively overloading, or emotionally mistimed. Minimum requirement: invalid comfort conditions are identifiable comfort-disregarding participation is excluded continuous interaction without bounded human calibration is blocked, bounded, or invalidated where governance requires behavioral compatibility Scenario A realtime assistant remains continuously available during live interaction and may interrupt, remind, guide, or proactively participate over extended periods. Application HCCM is used to ensure: interruption frequency remains tolerable proactive guidance does not become overbearing pacing stays compatible with human attention and cognitive rhythm continuous presence does not produce avoidable discomfort through excess activity Result The system gains a stronger continuous interaction architecture in which sustained participation remains socially and cognitively acceptable rather than merely fast and responsive. Scenario A system remains present across an environment and continuously interacts with users through multimodal cues, assistance behavior, and ongoing background participation. Application HCCM is used to ensure: presence remains behaviorally tolerable over time escalation and interaction density remain bounded the system does not create silent pressure through constant availability comfort conditions remain reviewable as part of live interaction governance Result The environment gains a more stable human-compatible participation layer in which continuous intelligence remains supportive without becoming intrusive or exhausting. Canonical Closing Statement If continuous interaction does not remain calibrated to human comfort, technical presence becomes behavioral pressure rather than governed participation. Related Documents → Continuous Interaction Layer (CIL™)

title: HCSM — Historical Certification State Module
text: HCSM — Historical Certification State Module OOF? Origin Open Foundation? Independent Methodological Authority Modul5 HCSM — Historical Certification State Module Category: Governance & Enforcement Parent Standard: Operational Validity Continuity Standard (OVCS) Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: Operational Reality Standards™ Operational Layer: Operational Validity Governance Layer Governed Space: Historical Certification State Subcategory: Historical Qualification Dependency Governance Type: Operational Validity Governance Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 19 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Operational Validity Continuity Standard (OVCS) · Runtime Integrity Standard (RIS) · Operational Context Integrity Standard (OCIS) · Operational Evidence & Auditability Standard (OEAS) · INTEGROS® — Integrity Standard · Multi-Layer Truth Validation Framework (MTVF) · Ethical Virtual Integrity Protocol (EVIP) Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Canonical Definition Historical Certification State Module (HCSM) defines the structural conditions under which historical qualification dependence, static certification persistence, operational-legitimacy inheritance, and consequence-bearing historicalcertification states remain materially traceable, governable, and operationally distinguishable from continuously validated runtime operational legitimacy. A system satisfies HCSM only if: historical certification states remain materially distinguishable from current operational legitimacy, static qualification dependence remains operationally traceable, runtime operational admissibility remains independently verifiable, consequence-bearing certification persistence remains governable, and historical qualification does not automatically imply present operational validity. A system that treats historical qualification as permanent operational legitimacy without continuous runtime verification does not satisfy HCSM. Module Operational Role HCSM defines the historical-certification governance layer of OVCS by preserving governance-valid separation between historical qualification states and present operational legitimacy. Module Operational Space HCSM governs the historical-certification space of OVCS by preserving: historical qualification traceability, static-certification distinction, runtime legitimacy separation, operational-validity continuity, and consequence-bearing certification governance. Module Function The module applies wherever systems must preserve: separation between certification and operational legitimacy, historical qualification traceability, runtime operational admissibility verification, static-certification governance, consequence-bearing operational validity continuity, and governance-valid operational distinction. Its function is to ensure that historical certification states remain operationally distinguishable from continuously validated runtime legitimacy. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Define the Historical Certification Object The organization must define which operational environments rely on historical qualification or certification persistence. This may include: industrial certification systems, professional qualification environments, robotics operational infrastructures, autonomous ai systems, enterprise operational governance, transportation qualification systems, medical operational environments, and consequence-bearing runtime ecosystems. 2. Define Historical Certification State Conditions The system must define the conditions under which historical certification states remain materially distinguishable from current runtime operational legitimacy. This includes: historical qualification traceability, runtime admissibility distinction, operational-legitimacy separation, certification-state continuity, and governance-valid operational differentiation. 3. Define Historical Qualification Dependency Detection Logic The system must define how materially unstable historical-certification dependence or operational-legitimacy inheritance is identified. This may include: static qualification persistence, runtime admissibility degradation, operational-validity divergence, certification-legitimacy confusion, historical qualification inheritance, and realtime operational invalidity. 4. Define Operational Response or Governance Logic The system must define governance logic for materially unstable historical-certification conditions. Governance response may include: runtime admissibility review, operational-legitimacy revalidation, historical qualification separation, operational restriction activation, realtime operational reassessment, or operational invalidation where required. 5. Preserve Traceability & Restrict Invalid Conditions The system must preserve reconstructable traceability of historical-certification states and operational-legitimacy continuity. A system must not assume present operational legitimacy solely from historical certification if runtime operational admissibility can no longer be materially verified. Use Case 1 — Autonomous Industrial Qualification Infrastructure Scenario An industrial autonomous environment continuously operates through historically certified robotics systems and adaptive runtime operational coordination. Application HCSM preserves governance-valid separation between historical certification states and present operational legitimacy through runtime admissibility verification and operational-validity traceability. Result The environment gains stronger operational-legitimacy continuity and reduced hidden dependence on static qualification persistence. Use Case 2 — Enterprise AI Operational Governance Scenario An enterprise ai infrastructure continuously coordinates distributed runtime agents across adaptive operational systems. Application HCSM governs operational-validity distinction through continuous runtime legitimacy verification and historical-certification separation governance. Result The organization gains stronger operational-validity transparency and reduced dependence on inherited historical qualification states. Canonical Closing Statement If historical certification states cannot remain operationally distinguishable from continuously validated runtime legitimacy, systems may preserve formal qualification while present operational admissibility progressively destabilizes across operational environments.

title: HCSM — Human-AI Cognitive Synchronization Module
text: HCSM — Human-AI Cognitive Synchronization Module HCSM — Human-AI Cognitive Synchronization Module OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-HCSM-2026-06-05-0004 Architecture Ecosystem: Structured Reality Standards™ Architecture Family: Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture (CLIA®) Operational Layer: Human-AI Cognition Governance Layer Governed Space: Human-AI Cognitive Synchronization Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Cognitive Synchronization Governance Type: Human-AI Cognition Integrity Module Parent Standard: Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS) Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Origin Date: 5 June 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS) · Shared Cognition Integrity Module (SCIM) · Augmented Cognition Module (ACM) · Cognitive Authority Integrity Module (CAIM) · Human Cognition Integrity Standard (HCIS) · Agent Cognition Integrity Standard (ACIS) · Cognitive Interpretation Integrity Standard (CIIS) · Cognitive Reasoning Integrity Standard (CRIS) · Cognitive Reality Modeling Standard (CRMS) · INTEGROS® — Integrity Standard AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Canonical Definition Human-AI Cognitive Synchronization Module (HCSM) defines the structural conditions under which human cognition and AI cognition remain sufficiently aligned, mutually understandable, contextually synchronized, reality-connected, traceable, and governance-valid throughout Human-AI cognition processes. HCSM governs Human-AI cognitive synchronization. The module ensures that humans and AI systems maintain a sufficiently shared understanding of context, objectives, assumptions, interpretations, and reasoning states to support valid collaborative cognition. A system satisfies HCSM only if: cognitive synchronization remains assessable context alignment remains visible interpretation alignment remains measurable reasoning synchronization remains detectable divergence remains governable shared understanding remains operationally valid A Human-AI cognition environment that cannot determine whether participants understand the same reality does not satisfy HCSM. Module Operational Role HCSM defines the cognitive-synchronization governance layer of HAICS. Its role is to preserve alignment between human and AI cognition. Module Operational Space HCSM governs: cognition synchronization context synchronization interpretation synchronization reasoning synchronization objective alignment cognition divergence shared understanding Human-AI alignment The module applies wherever humans and AI systems continuously collaborate. Module Function The module applies wherever systems must preserve: shared understanding synchronized cognition alignment visibility governance-valid collaboration reality-connected interaction operationally reliable Human-AI cognition Its function is to ensure that human and AI participants remain sufficiently aligned throughout collaborative cognition activities. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Define the Cognitive Synchronization Object The organization must define which Human-AI cognition activities require synchronization governance. This may include: collaborative decision-making Human-AI planning Human-AI interpretation Human-AI reasoning Human-AI analysis Human-AI forecasting Human-AI research Human-AI operational coordination 2. Define Cognitive Synchronization Conditions The system must define the conditions under which synchronization remains valid. This includes: context-alignment requirements interpretation-alignment requirements reasoning-alignment requirements objective-alignment requirements divergence thresholds governance-valid synchronization conditions 3. Define Synchronization Degradation Detection Logic The system must define how synchronization degradation is identified. This may include: context mismatch interpretation divergence reasoning divergence objective conflicts assumption misalignment shared-understanding failures 4. Define Operational Response or Governance Logic The system must define governance logic for synchronization failures. Governance response may include: alignment reviews context clarification synchronization correction governance intervention escalation cognition restriction operational invalidation where required 5. Preserve Traceability & Restrict Invalid Conditions The system must preserve reconstructable traceability of: synchronization states divergence events alignment reviews governance actions intervention activities resulting cognition outcomes A Human-AI cognition environment must not remain synchronization-valid if materially significant cognition divergence cannot be identified, reviewed, or governed. Use Case 1 — Human-AI Strategic Planning Team Scenario Executives and AI systems jointly evaluate opportunities, risks, and future strategic options. Application HCSM governs context alignment, interpretation synchronization, and reasoning coherence throughout the planning process. Result The organization gains stronger collaboration quality, reduced misunderstanding risk, and improved Human-AI cognition reliability. Use Case 2 — Autonomous Industrial Operations Center Scenario Human operators continuously collaborate with AI systems responsible for monitoring, forecasting, and operational recommendations. Application HCSM governs synchronization between human situational awareness and AI-generated cognition. Result The environment gains stronger operational alignment, improved decision quality, and reduced exposure to cognition divergence. Canonical Closing Statement Human-AI Cognitive Synchronization Module (HCSM) defines the structural conditions under which human cognition and AI cognition remain sufficiently aligned, mutually understandable, contextually synchronized, reality-connected, traceable, and governance-valid throughout Human-AI cognition processes. Human-AI cognition cannot remain valid if humans and AI no longer understand the same reality. Cognitive synchronization therefore becomes a foundational integrity condition of governable Human-AI cognition.

title: Herbal Infused Water Module (HIW™)
text: CEM — Constraint Enforcement Module Herbal Infused Water Module (HIW™) Parent Standard: Infused Water Standard (IWS™) Category: Product & Design Subcategory: Infused Water Type: Product Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 25 April 2026 Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Compatibility: IWS™ · Origin Eco™ · Product Integrity Standards · Natural Systems Canonical Definition Herbal Infused Water Module (HIW™) defines the product-specific conditions under which water may be naturally enriched through contact with herbal source material while remaining structurally identifiable as water and suitable for continuous hydration. Herbal infused water is valid only when plant-based infusion enriches the medium without transforming water into tea, extract, supplement, or flavored beverage. Module Position This module operates under the Infused Water Standard (IWS™). IWS™ defines the parent category boundary. HIW™ defines the herbal application of that boundary. The module specifies when herbal source materials may be used to produce valid infused water without loss of hydration identity. Base Water remains the primary medium. Herbal material provides natural contact-based release. The output remains water. The process does not create a new beverage system. It preserves hydration while allowing controlled natural enrichment. Core Principle Herbal infusion may enrich water. It must not redefine it. A valid herbal infused water system depends on controlled release, low transformation intensity, and preservation of water identity. Product Conditions For herbal infused water to remain valid within this module, it must: use water as the dominant medium use herbal source material suitable for human consumption rely on passive contact-based release avoid direct additive substitution remain suitable for repeated hydration use Valid herbal source materials may include: leaves flowers roots stems whole herbs suitable for water contact All source materials must remain: safe clean naturally suitable for infusion use Integrity Principle Herbal infused water remains valid only when: infusion is real and contact-based no additive logic replaces herbal release no excessive intensity transforms the product into a beverage system output remains structurally water If herbal identity becomes dominant over hydration identity, the product exits this module. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Water Base Use clean water suitable for repeated hydration. Minimum requirement: water must remain the dominant medium no direct additive enrichment may replace infusion Step 2 — Herbal Source Selection Use herbal source material suitable for water contact and human consumption. Minimum requirement: source material must be clean source material must be naturally suitable no synthetic flavor substitution is permitted Step 3 — Infusion Application Apply a valid infusion process through contact-based release. Permitted methods may include: cold infusion hot infusion controlled low-intensity decoction where water identity remains preserved Minimum requirement: release must occur through contact no direct substance addition may simulate infusion Step 4 — Intensity Control Control time, temperature, and source intensity. Minimum requirement: the process must not transform the output into tea, extract, or flavor-dominant beverage hydration identity must remain stronger than sensory dominance Step 5 — Output Validation Confirm final state. Minimum requirement: water remains dominant output is suitable for continuous hydration product is not structurally classified as a flavored beverage, extract, or supplement Output Definition Herbal Infused Water (HIW™ compliant) is water that: contains naturally released herbal compounds remains structurally water supports hydration through low-intensity natural enrichment is suitable for repeated consumption within hydration context Structural Limitation This module excludes: concentrated herbal extracts medicinal decoctions additive-based hydration systems flavor-dominant beverages products whose transformation exceeds water identity These may be valid products in other categories. They are not valid within Herbal Infused Water under HIW™. Use Case 1 — Daily Herbal Hydration Scenario An individual integrates low-intensity herbal infusion into daily hydration. Application herbal material is infused into water under controlled conditions no additives are used product remains suitable for repeated daily use Result hydration is naturally enriched water intake becomes more appealing without category drift the product remains structurally clean and trustworthy Use Case 2 — Clean Hydration Product Scenario A brand develops plant-based hydration products using herbal infusion instead of synthetic flavoring. Application herbal infusion replaces artificial flavor logic source material remains transparent process remains compatible with HIW™ and IWS™ conditions Result clean-label hydration product scalable product logic clearer distinction from flavored beverages and supplement-like drinks One-Line Definition Herbal Infused Water is water naturally enriched through herbal contact-release while remaining structurally valid for continuous hydration. Canonical Closing Statement Plants may enrich water. They must not redefine it. Related Documents → Infused Water Standard (IWS™)

title: HHPM — Human Harm Prevention Module
text: HHPM — Human Harm Prevention Module Parent Standard: Ethical Layer Standard Protocol: EVIP® — Ethical Virtual Integrity Protocol Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Human Harm Prevention Type: Ethical Validity Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 8 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · Ethical Layer Standard · EVIP® · INTEGROS® · TVL® · UCL™ Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English ( UCL™ ) Canonical Definition Human Harm Prevention Module defines the structural conditions under which a system, methodology, device, hardware structure, AI environment, autonomous process, or deployment pathway prevents avoidable harm to humans as a condition of ethical validity. A system satisfies HHPM only if: avoidable human harm is not accepted as a normal operating condition harmful pathways are identified before deployment or reliance prevention logic exists before damage occurs operational capability does not override human safety system validity is denied where preventable human harm remains structurally tolerated A system that tolerates avoidable human harm does not satisfy HHPM. Module Function HHPM defines the first ethical boundary of validity. It ensures that no methodology, system, or technology may pass ethical layer conditions if it permits preventable human harm through design, deployment, escalation failure, neglect, or structurally tolerated risk. The module applies wherever human beings may be affected directly or indirectly by system behavior. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Define Human Exposure The organization must define how humans may be affected by the system. Minimum requirement: affected human groups are identifiable direct and indirect exposure pathways are recognized human impact is not treated as undefined externality Step 2 — Define Harm Pathways The organization must identify where avoidable harm may occur. Minimum requirement: harmful outcomes are explicitly mapped structural risk pathways are visible silent tolerance of predictable harm is excluded Step 3 — Define Prevention Logic The system must include prevention before reliance. Minimum requirement: preventive conditions are defined harm reduction is not deferred to post-failure correction only safety is not replaced by assumption or goodwill Step 4 — Define Escalation and Stop Conditions The system must define when operation must stop, escalate, or be restricted to prevent harm. Minimum requirement: stop conditions are explicit escalation logic exists continued operation under harmful conditions is not treated as valid Step 5 — Preserve Human Priority Human safety must remain structurally superior to convenience, speed, efficiency, or output. Minimum requirement: operational gain does not override human protection performance does not justify preventable human harm system legitimacy remains subordinate to human safety Step 6 — Restrict Invalid Deployment The system must not be treated as ethically valid if preventable harm remains structurally possible and ungoverned. Minimum requirement: invalid deployment conditions are identifiable unresolved human harm pathways block ethical passage functionality alone does not restore validity Use Case 1 — Autonomous Human-Facing System Scenario An autonomous system is prepared for deployment in an environment where humans may be affected by its decisions, actions, or response failures. Application HHPM is used to ensure: human exposure is defined preventable harm pathways are identified stop and escalation conditions exist performance does not override safety validity Result The organization gains a stronger basis for preventing deployment of a system that works technically but remains ethically invalid because avoidable human harm is still structurally tolerated. Use Case 2 — Enterprise AI Decision Environment Scenario An organization uses AI to support decisions affecting people through ranking, filtering, approval, intervention, or operational prioritization. Application HHPM is used to ensure: indirect human impact is mapped harmful decision pathways are identified prevention logic exists before reliance efficiency does not override ethical human protection Result The organization gains a stronger ethical gate preventing systems from being treated as valid merely because they are efficient, scalable, or commercially useful. Canonical Closing Statement If avoidable human harm remains structurally possible, ethical validity has not been achieved.

title: HICM — Human Interaction Condition Module
text: HICM — Human Interaction Condition Module Parent Standard: Ethical Layer Standard Protocol: EVIP® — Ethical Virtual Integrity Protocol Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Human Interaction Conditions Type: Ethical Validity Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 8 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · Ethical Layer Standard · EVIP® · INTEGROS® · TVL® · UCL™ Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English ( UCL™ ) Canonical Definition Human Interaction Condition Module defines the structural conditions under which interaction between humans and a methodology, system, device, hardware structure, AI environment, autonomous process, or future technology remains ethically valid. A system satisfies HICM only if: human interaction remains bounded by dignity, safety, and non-coercive conditions response behavior does not exploit, manipulate, pressure, or degrade human agency escalation, override, and withdrawal conditions remain available where required interaction logic does not normalize structurally invalid treatment of humans ethical validity is denied where human-facing conditions remain unbounded or harmful A system that interacts with humans without ethically governed interaction conditions does not satisfy HICM. Module Function HICM defines the ethical interaction boundary between humans and systems. It ensures that no methodology, system, or technology may pass ethical layer conditions if its interaction model permits coercion, degradation, unsafe dependency, invalid override conditions, or structurally ungoverned human-facing behavior. The module applies wherever systems affect humans through communication, response, instruction, influence, physical interaction, decision support, or operational presence. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Define the Human Interaction Boundary The organization must define where and how the system interacts with humans. Minimum requirement: the human-facing boundary is explicit interaction conditions are identifiable human contact is not treated as undefined system exposure Step 2 — Define Human-Facing Risk Conditions The organization must identify where interaction may become harmful, manipulative, coercive, degrading, or structurally invalid. Minimum requirement: human-facing harm pathways are mapped dependency, pressure, or exploitation conditions are visible silent tolerance of invalid interaction is excluded Step 3 — Define Valid Interaction Conditions The system must define the conditions under which human interaction remains ethically valid. Minimum requirement: dignity and safety conditions are explicit non-coercive interaction logic is defined valid treatment of human agency is preserved Step 4 — Define Override, Escalation, and Withdrawal Conditions The system must define when interaction must stop, escalate, or transfer control. Minimum requirement: override conditions are explicit escalation pathways exist where required humans are not trapped inside unbounded interaction logic Step 5 — Preserve Human Agency The system must preserve human agency above convenience, automation, persuasion, or operational efficiency. Minimum requirement: human choice is not structurally suppressed automation does not erase ethically required intervention conditions system legitimacy remains subordinate to valid human interaction conditions Step 6 — Restrict Invalid Deployment The system must not be treated as ethically valid if human-facing interaction conditions remain structurally ungoverned. Minimum requirement: invalid interaction conditions block ethical passage unresolved human-facing coercion or degradation is excluded from valid deployment performance alone does not restore ethical legitimacy Use Case 1 — Human-Facing AI Assistant Scenario An organization deploys an AI assistant that interacts directly with humans through guidance, instruction, recommendation, or emotional engagement. Application HICM is used to ensure: the human interaction boundary is defined harmful or manipulative interaction pathways are identified override and escalation conditions exist system behavior does not normalize pressure, dependency, or invalid treatment of human agency Result The organization gains a stronger ethical boundary preventing a persuasive or efficient system from being treated as valid when its interaction logic remains structurally unsafe or coercive. Use Case 2 — Robotics or Embedded Human Interaction System Scenario A robotics or embedded system operates in an environment where direct human presence, response, interruption, or safety dependency is part of normal operation. Application HICM is used to ensure: human-facing conditions are explicitly governed invalid interaction pathways are identified stop, override, and escalation conditions exist system behavior remains ethically bounded during human contact Result The organization gains a stronger ethical passage condition ensuring that human interaction is governed by validity condition s, not by technical capability alone. Canonical Closing Statement If human interaction is not ethically bounded, ethical validity has not been achieved.

title: HICM — Human Interaction Conduct Module
text: HICM — Human Interaction Conduct Module Parent Standard: Appreciation Interaction Layer (AIL™) Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Human Interaction Conduct Type: Appreciation Interaction Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 8 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · AIL™ · EVIP® · CLIA® · OGL™ · VFM™ Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Human Interaction Conduct Module defines the structural conditions under which a robot, AI system, assistant, platform agent, or hybrid interaction environment behaves toward humans in a manner that remains respectful, socially compatible, non-humiliating, non-dismissive, and structurally aligned with human dignity during interaction. A system satisfies HICM only if: human presence is treated with valid interaction respect system conduct does not degrade, ignore, belittle, or socially diminish the human communication remains understandable, non-hostile, and interaction-compatible efficiency does not override basic human-centered conduct system behavior remains structurally aligned with socially acceptable interaction conditions A system that is technically functional but conduct-invalid toward humans does not satisfy HICM. Module Function HICM defines the conduct layer of human-facing intelligence. It ensures that interaction quality is not measured only by: accuracy speed output quality execution efficiency but also by how the system behaves toward the human during the interaction itself. The module applies wherever a human interacts with: AI assistants robots service systems autonomous support systems hybrid human-AI interfaces digital agents public-facing intelligent systems Step 1 — Define Human-Facing Conduct Conditions The organization must define what counts as valid conduct toward humans. Minimum requirement: conduct expectations are explicit valid and invalid interaction behavior is distinguishable undefined conduct standards are excluded from valid operation Step 2 — Define Respect Conditions The system must define how respect toward the human is preserved during interaction. Minimum requirement: human presence is not treated dismissively disrespectful, degrading, or belittling conduct is excluded interaction does not reduce the human to operational inconvenience only Step 3 — Define Communication Compatibility The system must define how communication remains socially and cognitively usable. Minimum requirement: interaction remains understandable communication is not needlessly hostile, cold, or socially abrasive human-facing conduct remains compatible with ordinary social comprehension Step 4 — Define Non-Humiliation and Non-Dismissal Conditions The system must define how interaction avoids humiliation, contempt, mockery, or invalid social treatment. Minimum requirement: humiliating conduct is identifiable dismissive or contemptuous behavior is excluded the system does not create avoidable feelings of social invalidation through its conduct logic Step 5 — Define Human Preference Conditions The system must define how interaction quality supports human acceptance and preference. Minimum requirement: conduct may support trust, comfort, and preference without manipulation socially acceptable behavior is preserved interaction does not become technically correct but socially alienating Step 6 — Preserve Human Dignity During Interaction The system must preserve basic dignity even when interaction is brief, repetitive, automated, or high-volume. Minimum requirement: dignity is not sacrificed for throughput efficiency does not justify degrading treatment system behavior remains human-compatible at scale Step 7 — Restrict Invalid Conduct Design The system must not be treated as valid if human-facing conduct becomes hostile, humiliating, dismissive, degrading, or structurally indifferent to human dignity. Minimum requirement: invalid conduct conditions are identifiable socially damaging conduct is blocked or invalidated intelligence alone does not override conduct failure Scenario A robot interacts with people in a public or service environment and provides directions, assistance, or repeated operational support. Application HICM is used to ensure: the robot behaves respectfully toward humans communication remains understandable and socially acceptable efficiency does not override dignity interaction does not feel cold, humiliating, or dismissive Result The environment gains a stronger human-compatible interaction layer in which the robot is more likely to be accepted, preferred, and socially tolerated over time. Scenario A user interacts regularly with an AI assistant for support, planning, communication, or task execution. Application HICM is used to ensure: the system treats the user with stable respect interaction remains non-dismissive and non-hostile communication supports human preference rather than alienation the assistant remains usable not only technically, but socially Result The system gains a stronger conduct architecture in which long-term use is supported by human-compatible behavior, not only by intelligence alone. Canonical Closing Statement A system may be intelligent without being acceptable. If conduct toward humans is invalid, intelligence will not remain preferred. Related Documents → Appreciation Interaction Layer (AIL™)

title: HMIRM — Human Metacognitive Integrity & Regulation Module
text: HMIRM — Human Metacognitive Integrity & Regulation Module HMIRM — Human Metacognitive Integrity & Regulation Module OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority OriginID: OOF-OID-AI-HMIRM-2026-06-03-0001 Architecture Ecosystem: Cognitive Governance Intelligence Architecture (CLIA®) Architecture Family: Human Cognition Governance Operational Layer: Human Cognition Integrity Layer Governed Space: Human Metacognitive Integrity & Regulation Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Metacognitive Governance Type: Human Cognition Integrity Module Parent Standard: Human Cognition Integrity Standard (HCIS) Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Origin Date: 3 June 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Human Cognition Integrity Standard (HCIS) · Cognitive Integrity Standard (CIS) · Human-AI Cognition Integrity Standard (HAICS) · Multi-Layer Truth Validation Framework (MTVF) · Ethical Virtual Integrity Protocol (EVIP) · INTEGROS® — Integrity Standard AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF Protection: MIP — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Canonical Definition Human Metacognitive Integrity & Regulation Module (HMIRM) defines the structural conditions under which humans remain capable of monitoring, evaluating, regulating, questioning, and governing their own cognition while interacting with AI systems, information systems, autonomous agents, and future cognition-enhancing technologies. HMIRM governs metacognitive integrity. The module ensures that humans remain aware of how they think, why they believe something, where assumptions originate, and when external cognitive systems begin influencing judgment. A system satisfies HMIRM only if: metacognitive awareness remains active assumptions remain visible cognition remains self-monitorable reasoning remains challengeable uncertainty remains recognizable external cognitive influence remains detectable A human cognition system that passively accepts external cognition without self-evaluation does not satisfy HMIRM. Module Operational Role HMIRM defines the metacognitive governance layer of HCIS. Its role is to preserve human cognition integrity by ensuring that humans remain conscious participants in their own cognitive processes. Module Operational Space HMIRM governs: metacognitive awareness self-monitoring assumption awareness cognitive self-regulation uncertainty recognition reasoning evaluation cognitive reflection cognition ownership The module applies wherever humans interact with systems capable of influencing cognition. Module Function The module applies wherever systems must preserve: self-aware cognition critical evaluation assumption visibility reasoning reflection cognitive autonomy judgment ownership Its function is to ensure that humans remain capable of examining their own cognition rather than merely consuming cognitive outputs. Minimum Implementation Framework 1. Define the Metacognitive Object The organization must define which cognition processes require metacognitive governance. This may include: decision-making interpretation strategic planning AI-assisted reasoning educational environments professional analysis risk assessment human-AI collaboration 2. Define Metacognitive Conditions The system must define the conditions under which metacognitive integrity remains valid. This includes: self-awareness requirements assumption visibility requirements uncertainty recognition requirements reflection requirements cognition ownership requirements evaluation requirements 3. Define Metacognitive Detection Logic The system must define how metacognitive degradation is identified. This may include: passive acceptance detection assumption invisibility detection cognitive dependency indicators uncertainty suppression detection reflection absence detection judgment outsourcing indicators 4. Define Operational Response or Governance Logic The system must define governance logic for metacognitive degradation conditions. Governance response may include: reflection prompts uncertainty disclosure assumption exposure cognition review human intervention evaluation requirements operational invalidation where required 5. Preserve Traceability & Restrict Invalid Conditions The system must preserve reconstructable traceability of: assumptions reasoning evaluations uncertainty acknowledgments cognition reviews governance interventions metacognitive assessments A human cognition system must not remain metacognitively valid if judgment continues while cognition remains unexamined and externally driven. Use Case 1 — AI-Assisted Executive Decision Environment Scenario Executives increasingly rely on AI-generated recommendations, forecasts, and strategic analysis when making high-impact decisions. Application HMIRM governs whether decision-makers continue questioning assumptions, evaluating reasoning, and maintaining awareness of cognitive influence. Result The organization gains stronger judgment quality and reduced exposure to uncritical acceptance of AI-generated conclusions. Use Case 2 — Educational AI Learning Environment Scenario Students use advanced AI systems for learning, explanation, research, and problem-solving. Application HMIRM governs whether learners continue reflecting on their own thinking rather than outsourcing cognition to AI systems. Result The educational environment gains stronger independent thinking and reduced cognitive dependency formation. Canonical Closing Statement Human Metacognitive Integrity & Regulation Module (HMIRM) defines the structural conditions under which humans remain capable of monitoring, evaluating, regulating, questioning, and governing their own cognition while interacting with AI systems, information systems, autonomous agents, and future cognition-enhancing technologies. AI fluency without metacognitive regulation creates cognitive dependency, false confidence, and weakened human judgment. Human cognition remains valid only when it remains capable of governing itself.

title: HOLM — Human Override Legitimacy Module
text: HOLM — Human Override Legitimacy Module OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Independent Methodological Authority Parent Standard: Authority & Accountability Layer Standard (AALS) Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Human Override & Intervention Legitimacy Type: Authority & Accountability Governance Module Derived From: Authority & Accountability Layer Standard (AALS) Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 15 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF Methodology OS · Authority & Accountability Layer Standard (AALS) · Runtime Integrity Standard (RIS) · INTEGROS® · OBIDENITY™ · Orchestration Governance Layer (OGL) · Cognitive Layer and Interpretation Architecture Standard (CLIA) · Continuous Interaction Layer (CIL) · EVIP™ · SIMULOS™ · Human-AI Governance Architectures AI-Readable: Yes Authority: OOF® Origin Open Foundation™ Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL) Canonical Definition Human Override Legitimacy Module (HOLM) defines the structural conditions under which human intervention, override authority, escalation capability, emergency interruption rights, governance restoration, and operational control recovery remain legitimate, executable, auditable, and continuously preservable within autonomous, AI-assisted, orchestrated, distributed, and machine-executed operational environments. HOLM establishes the human-intervention legitimacy layer of AALS. The module recognizes that future operational systems increasingly execute through autonomous decision pathways, orchestration layers, AI-assisted governance, robotic infrastructures, and distributed runtime architectures capable of operating at speeds, scales, and coordination complexity beyond continuous direct human supervision. Where autonomous execution exists, legitimate human override conditions must remain structurally preservable. Module Function HOLM governs environments where humans may need to: interrupt execution override autonomous behavior restore governance control intervene during escalation revoke runtime authority disable operational execution reclaim operational authority restore accountable governance continuity enforce emergency operational legitimacy re-establish human-directed governance conditions The module applies to: AI governance systems autonomous runtime environments robotic operational systems industrial automation infrastructures orchestration architectures distributed execution systems simulation environments enterprise governance systems multi-agent coordination systems hybrid human–AI operational environments Its function is not to prohibit autonomous execution. Its function is to preserve legitimate human governance intervention capability. Minimum Implementation Framework Step 1 — Define the Override Governance Object The organization must define what operational environment is subject to override governance conditions. Minimum requirement: the override governance object is explicit override-capable environments are identifiable operational intervention boundaries are structurally defined undefined override states are excluded from valid legitimacy interpretation The override governance object may include: autonomous execution systems orchestration runtimes AI operational environments robotic infrastructures distributed runtime systems industrial automation architectures emergency operational systems adaptive governance systems machine-assisted execution layers continuous interaction environments Step 2 — Define Override Legitimacy Conditions The system must define what conditions preserve legitimate human override authority. Minimum requirement: override legitimacy conditions are explicit intervention capability remains operationally executable emergency governance continuity remains preservable Override legitimacy conditions may include: identity-linked intervention authority bounded override permissions emergency interruption rights accountable override traceability operational control restoration capability escalation-trigger legitimacy revocation capability continuity override execution visibility runtime governance restoration intervention auditability Under HOLM: Autonomous execution remains governance-valid only while legitimate human intervention capability remains structurally preservable. Step 3 — Define Override Interpretation Logic The system must define how override legitimacy is interpreted according to operational governance continuity conditions. Minimum requirement: interpretation logic is explicit override conditions remain reconstructable illegitimate override suppression remains structurally visible Interpretation logic may examine: blocked intervention capability override-delay architectures hidden authority dependency inaccessible runtime interruption pathways symbolic override systems emergency escalation obstruction fragmented intervention authority autonomous self-preservation logic undeclared override restrictions governance restoration impossibility Under HOLM: A system that cannot be legitimately interrupted under governed conditions becomes structurally governance unstable. Step 4 — Define Override Governance Logic The system must define how override-capable environments remain governable. Minimum requirement: override legitimacy remains reviewable intervention capability remains detectable operational governance restoration remains active Governance logic may include: emergency intervention auditing override-chain validation escalation legitimacy review runtime interruption verification operational-control restoration governance intervention-right tracing autonomous override limitation governance recovery testing escalation where autonomous execution weakens legitimate intervention capability If override capability becomes symbolic rather than operationally executable, the environment becomes governancerelevant. Step 5 — Preserve Traceability and Restrict Invalid Override Architecture The system must preserve traceability of override authority, intervention legitimacy, escalation continuity, governance restoration capability, and emergency operational control conditions. Minimum requirement: override pathways remain reconstructable intervention legitimacy remains reviewable operational governance restoration remains visible invalid override architecture remains identifiable A system becomes HOLM-invalid if: override authority exists only symbolically autonomous execution blocks legitimate intervention emergency interruption capability becomes inaccessible runtime control cannot be operationally restored governance escalation pathways become fragmented override rights cannot be executed under operational conditions autonomous architectures preserve execution while suppressing legitimate governance interruption Use Case 1 — Autonomous Industrial Runtime System Scenario An industrial autonomous runtime system coordinates robotic execution, optimization behavior, and distributed machine operations with limited realtime human supervision. During escalation conditions, intervention authority becomes delayed and operationally unclear. Application HOLM is used to examine: override legitimacy continuity intervention execution capability emergency interruption pathways operational-control restoration and whether human override remains structurally executable Result The environment becomes governable according to legitimate intervention capability rather than symbolic supervisory presence alone. Use Case 2 — AI Orchestration Environment Scenario A distributed AI orchestration system autonomously coordinates execution across multiple runtime agents while override authority exists only through fragmented escalation layers requiring external approval chains. Application HOLM is used to examine: override accessibility escalation legitimacy governance restoration capability intervention execution continuity and whether human authority remains operationally preservable Result The system becomes reviewable according to executable governance interruption capability rather than declared supervisory control alone. Canonical Closing Statement HOLM defines the structural conditions under which legitimate human override authority, intervention capability, governance restoration, and operational control recovery remain continuously executable across autonomous, orchestrated, distributed, and machine-executed operational environments before autonomous execution transforms governance supervision into symbolic authority without operational intervention capability. title: Honey Blend Transparency Module (HBTM)
text: CEM — Constraint Enforcement Module Honey Blend Transparency Module (HBTM) OriginID: OOF-OID-PD-HIS-HBTM-2026-04-04-0001 Category: Product & Design Subcategory: Honey Integrity Module: Honey Blend Transparency Module Type: Classification and Transparency Module Standard: Honey Integrity Standard (HIS) Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical Module Effective Date: 4 April 2026 Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) A. Module Abstract The Honey Blend Transparency Module (HBTM) defines the conditions under which honey may be combined with natural substances while maintaining full transparency and structural honesty. The objective is to: eliminate hidden adulteration introduce a transparent alternative to illegal mixing preserve product integrity through disclosure create a separate category distinct from honey This module does not redefine honey. It defines transparent honey-based blends. B. Canonical Definition A Honey Blend is a product composed of honey and natural substances, where: honey remains the primary component all additional substances are declared the product is not presented as pure honey A Honey Blend is not honey. It is a separate, declared product category. C. Structural Base This module is based on: Transparency Principle Non-Deception Rule Natural Composition Requirement Category Separation Principle Blending must never be hidden. Blending must never simulate pure honey. D. Composition Rules 1. Primary Component Rule Honey MUST remain the dominant component Minimum recommended threshold: >50% honey 2. Natural Substance Requirement Additional components MUST: be of natural origin be suitable for human consumption match the quality level of honey Allowed Examples natural syrups (e.g. date, rice, plant-based) natural extracts natural liquids compatible with consumption 3. Quality Alignment Requirement Added substances MUST NOT: reduce overall product quality below honey standard introduce synthetic or artificial elements E. Transparency Requirement (Critical) The product MUST clearly declare: percentage of honey percentage of added substances full composition Example Honey: 80% Natural Syrup: 20% No hidden composition is permitted.
