title: MIF — Earned Learning Implementation Framework
text: MIF — Earned Learning Implementation Framework MIF — Earned Learning Implementation Framework Standard: Earned Learning Standard (ELS) Category: Systems & Product Subcategory: Learning & Skill Systems Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Effective Date: 15 April 2026 Purpose This framework defines the minimum structure required to implement earned learning in real environments. It ensures that learning is based on demonstrated ability, not assumed knowledge. Implementation Principle Learning must be proven through action before progression is allowed. Core Implementation Loop All implementations MUST follow: Teach → Challenge → Demonstrate → Validate → Unlock Implementation Layers 1. Instruction Layer Introduce a concept in its simplest functional form. 2. Challenge Layer Present a task or real-world scenario requiring application. 3. Demonstration Layer Require the learner to perform the task. 4. Validation Layer Verify correctness, functionality, or effectiveness. 5. Progression Layer Unlock reward or next stage only after validation. Implementation Steps Step 1 — Define Learning Unit Break knowledge into actionable components. Step 2 — Assign Challenge Create a task that requires application. Step 3 — Require Demonstration Ensure the learner performs the task. Step 4 — Validate Outcome Confirm that the result is correct. Step 5 — Unlock Progression Allow advancement only after proof. Minimum Implementation Requirement A system satisfies ELS only if: learning requires application performance is demonstrated outcomes are validated progression is earned Failure Condition If any of the following occurs: no demonstration no validation automatic progression reward without proof → learning integrity is invalid. System Output A system implementing ELS produces: demonstrated capability measurable performance reliable skill development Compatibility Compatible with: OOF Methodology OS ORGS Canonical Closing Statement Learning must be proven or it does not exist.

title: MIF — Execution Layer Implementation Framework
text: MIF — Execution Layer Implementation Framework MIF — Execution Layer Implementation Framework Standard: Execution Layer — Enforcement Standard Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Execution & Enforcement Systems Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Effective Date: 15 April 2026 Purpose This framework defines the full operational implementation of controlled execution within a system. It ensures that all actions are authorized, traceable, constrained, consistent, and bound to outcomes. Implementation Principle Execution must be fully governed from authority to outcome. Execution Lifecycle All execution MUST follow this sequence: Authority → Execution → Constraint → Integrity → Trace → Outcome System Architecture Execution Layer operates through five integrated modules: Authority & Permission (APM) Execution Trace (ETM) Constraint Enforcement (CEM) Execution Integrity (EIM) Outcome Binding (OBM) All modules MUST operate simultaneously. Implementation Layers 1. Authority Layer (APM) Define who or what can act and under what permissions. 2. Trace Layer (ETM) Record all execution data including actor, time, and context. 3. Constraint Layer (CEM) Enforce boundaries and prevent out-of-scope actions. 4. Integrity Layer (EIM) Ensure execution remains consistent and unmodified. 5. Outcome Layer (OBM) Bind all outputs directly to execution. Implementation Steps Step 1 — Define Authority Identify all actors and assign permissions. Step 2 — Initialize Execution Start execution under defined authority. Step 3 — Enforce Constraints Apply rules and boundaries in real time. Step 4 — Monitor Integrity Detect deviations or manipulation. Step 5 — Record Execution Capture full trace of execution. Step 6 — Bind Outcome Link all outputs to execution. Minimum Implementation Requirement A system satisfies Execution Layer only if: all actions have defined authority all execution is traceable constraints are enforced execution integrity is maintained outcomes are bound to execution Failure Condition Execution is invalid if: authority is undefined execution is not traceable constraints are bypassed execution is altered outcomes are detached System Output A system implementing Execution Layer produces: controlled execution verifiable actions traceable system behavior valid and bound outcomes Compatibility Compatible with: OBIDENITY — Identity Layer INTEGROS — Integrity Standard MTVF — Truth Validation OOF Methodology OS ORGS Canonical Closing Statement Execution must be fully governed, or the system is not valid.

title: MIF — Minimum Implementation Framework (AHIM™)
text: CEM — Constraint Enforcement Module MIF — Minimum Implementation Framework (AHIM™) Module: AHIM™ — Agent Harness Integrity Module Parent Standard: Runtime Integrity Standard (RIS) Type: Minimum Implementation Framework Purpose This framework defines the minimum structural and operational conditions required to implement Agent Harness Integrity (AHIM™). It ensures that AI agent systems remain controlled, verifiable, and valid during real-time execution. Implementation Principle Execution must remain controlled, bounded, and verifiable at all times. Core Implementation Architecture A system implementing AHIM™ must establish six non-bypassable control layers: 1. Execution Boundary Layer The system must: define explicit execution boundaries prevent actions outside authorized scope enforce runtime constraints at all times 2. Tool Governance Layer The system must: define permitted tools and actions enforce authorization for all tool interactions ensure all tool usage is traceable 3. Memory Integrity Layer The system must: control read/write operations prevent unauthorized mutation maintain consistent and coherent state 4. Session Control Layer The system must: define session lifecycle and boundaries control state transitions prevent uncontrolled persistence 5. Environment Control Layer The system must: isolate execution environments prevent uncontrolled external effects ensure auditable system behavior 6. Outcome Verification Layer The system must: link outputs to execution context enforce constraint alignment enable auditability of all results Minimum Operational Requirements To be considered AHIM™ compliant, a system must: enforce all control layers simultaneously maintain real-time visibility into execution detect and prevent deviation from defined conditions ensure that all actions are attributable and traceable Implementation Steps Define execution scope and boundaries Establish tool authorization and governance Implement memory control mechanisms Define session lifecycle and limits Isolate and control execution environment Enable output traceability and verification Continuous Enforcement Condition All implementation layers must operate continuously during runtime. If any layer becomes inactive or bypassed, system integrity is invalid. Failure Condition Implementation is invalid if: execution boundaries are not enforced tool usage is uncontrolled memory state is inconsistent sessions are unbounded environment allows uncontrolled impact outputs cannot be verified System Output A valid AHIM™ implementation produces: controlled execution behavior traceable and auditable actions consistent runtime state verifiable outputs Canonical Closing Statement A system is not defined by how it is built, but by how it behaves during execution. If execution is not controlled, integrity does not exist. Related Documents → AHIM™ — Agent Harness Integrity Module → AHIM™ — Self-Declaration Framework → Runtime Integrity Standard (RIS)

title: Mineral Infused Water Module (MIW™)
text: CEM — Constraint Enforcement Module Mineral Infused Water Module (MIW™) Parent Standard: Infused Water Standard (IWS™) Category: Product & Design Subcategory: Infused Water Type: Product Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 25 April 2026 Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Compatibility: IWS™ · Origin Eco™ · Product Integrity Standards · Natural Systems Canonical Definition Mineral Infused Water Module (MIW™) defines the product-specific conditions under which water may be naturally enriched through contact with valid mineral source material while remaining structurally identifiable as water and suitable for continuous hydration. Mineral infused water is valid only when mineral enrichment occurs through natural contact-based release and does not transform water into a fortified, additive-based, or chemically modified product. Module Position This module operates under the Infused Water Standard (IWS™). IWS™ defines the parent hydration boundary. MIW™ defines the mineral application of that boundary. The module specifies when mineral source material may enrich water without replacing its identity as water. Base Water remains the primary medium. Mineral source material enables natural release through contact. The output remains water. The process does not create a supplement or chemically fortified liquid. It preserves hydration while allowing controlled mineral enrichment. Core Principle Mineral contact may enrich water. It must not redefine it. A valid mineral infused water system depends on passive release, structural restraint, and preservation of hydration identity. Product Conditions For mineral infused water to remain valid within this module, it must: use water as the dominant medium use natural mineral source material suitable for water contact rely on passive mineral release through contact avoid direct mineral addition or artificial fortification remain suitable for repeated hydration use Valid mineral source materials may include natural mineral-bearing materials suitable for controlled water contact under safe conditions. All source materials must remain: safe clean suitable for human use free from contamination and unsafe release behavior Integrity Principle Mineral infused water remains valid only when: enrichment occurs through real contact-based release no direct additive logic replaces mineral infusion no forced mineralization or chemical alteration is used output remains structurally water If mineral loading redefines the function or identity of water, the product exits this module. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Water Base Use clean water suitable for repeated hydration. Minimum requirement: water must remain the dominant medium no additive-based mineral fortification may replace infusion Step 2 — Mineral Source Selection Use mineral source material suitable for water contact and safe human use. Minimum requirement: source material must be naturally suitable source material must be clean and stable no unsafe contamination or uncontrolled release may be present Step 3 — Contact-Based Infusion Apply mineral enrichment through passive contact between water and mineral source material. Minimum requirement: release must occur through contact no direct addition of mineral substances may simulate infusion no artificial acceleration may replace natural release logic Step 4 — Intensity Control Control time, exposure, and contact conditions. Minimum requirement: enrichment must remain within hydration identity output must not become a supplement-like or chemically dominant liquid mineral presence must not override structural water identity Step 5 — Output Validation Confirm final state. Minimum requirement: water remains dominant output is suitable for continuous hydration product is not structurally classified as fortified water, supplement liquid, or chemically modified drink Output Definition Mineral Infused Water (MIW™ compliant) is water that: contains naturally released mineral compounds through contact remains structurally water supports hydration through controlled natural mineral enrichment is suitable for repeated consumption within hydration context Structural Limitation This module excludes: direct mineral fortification forced mineralization additive-based mineral drinks supplement-style hydration products products whose mineral intensity exceeds water identity These may be valid products in other categories. They are not valid within Mineral Infused Water under MIW™. Use Case 1 — Daily Mineral Hydration Scenario An individual uses naturally mineral-infused water as part of regular hydration. Application water is exposed to valid mineral source material under controlled conditions no direct additives are used the final product remains suitable for repeated daily hydration Result hydration is naturally enriched water remains structurally simple and clean mineral presence is achieved without conversion into supplement logic Use Case 2 — Natural Mineral Hydration Product Scenario A brand develops a hydration product based on natural mineral contact rather than additive-based fortification. Application mineral release occurs through contact-based process source material remains transparent output remains compatible with MIW™ and IWS™ conditions Result clean hydration product with natural mineral positioning clearer distinction from fortified drinks stronger category credibility through structural restraint One-Line Definition Mineral Infused Water is water naturally enriched through controlled mineral contact while remaining structurally valid for continuous hydration. Canonical Closing Statement Minerals may enrich water. They must not redefine it. Related Documents → Infused Water Standard (IWS™)

title: Minimal Implementation Framework (MIF)
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Minimal Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Input Recognition Identify the asset entering the system. Minimum requirement: identifiable asset defined input structure Step 2 — Validation Reference Confirm that the asset has passed a validation process. Minimum requirement: reference to validation source (MTVF or equivalent) traceable validation context Step 3 — Integrity Check Evaluate whether the asset shows signs of inconsistency or manipulation. Minimum requirement: structural consistency no detected anomalies Step 4 — Classification Assignment Assign one of three states: Verified Unverified Contaminated Step 5 — Decision Enforcement Apply system behavior based on classification: Verified → allow Unverified → restrict Contaminated → block Structural Rule No asset may enter a system without TSA classification. Closing Statement Modern systems operate on assumed trust. TSA replaces assumption with classification. Trust is not declared. Trust is validated and enforced.

title: Minimal Self- Declaration Framework
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Soil Integrity™ Minimal Self- Declaration Framework This framework provides a simple method for implementing the Soil Integrity™ Standard through transparent disclosure of soil-based production conditions. The framework is designed to be easy to apply by both small producers and larger production systems. No certification body is required. No external audit is required under the minimal level. The objective is structural transparency and declared responsibility. Implementation Steps Step 1 — Declare Soil Environment The producer identifies the soil environment used in production. Examples: Natural soil Mixed soil Artificial substrate Controlled environment soil system If multiple soil environments are used, each should be declared. Step 2 — Declare Fertilization Inputs The producer declares whether fertilization inputs are used. Declaration includes: Fertilization used: Yes / No If fertilization is used, the category should be declared. Examples: Animal manure Plant compost Mineral fertilizer Synthetic fertilizer Sewage-derived fertilizer No prohibition is imposed. Transparency is required. Step 3 — Declare Plant Protection Practices The producer declares whether plant protection substances are used. Declaration includes: Plant protection used: Yes / No The declared use should reflect the actual role of water in production. Examples: Frequency categories: Occasional Seasonal Regular Step 4 — Responsibility Declaration The producer publishes a short declaration confirming transparency of soil inputs. Example declaration: “This production is declared under the Soil Integrity™ Standard. Soil environment, fertilization inputs, and plant protection practices are transparently disclosed under producer responsibility.” The declaration may be published on a website on a product sheet on supplier documentation via QR code reference Documentation Requirements Implementation requires only: one soil disclosure sheet one input declaration one public responsibility statement No certification required. No external audit required under the minimal implementation level. Structural Value Soil Integrity™ transforms: hidden soil inputs into declared production transparency. This strengthens: buyer confidence supply chain clarity environmental accountability long-term production credibility Closing Principle Transparent soil inputs create credible soil-based production systems.

title: Minimal Self- Declaration Framework
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Origin Eco™ Minimal Self- Declaration Framework Framework Type: Implementation Framework Related Standard: Origin Eco™ Standard Version: 1.0 Purpose This framework provides a structured method enabling producers to declare alignment with the Origin Eco™ Standard through transparent disclosure of origin, materials, and production processes. The objective is to establish visible environmental transparency through producer responsibility. Implementation Principle Implementation of the Origin Eco™ Standard at the declaration level operates through public structural disclosure of origin, material composition, and production processes. Responsibility for the declaration remains with the declaring entity. Declaration Conditions A product or production process may be declared under the Origin Eco™ Standard when the following information is documented and publicly accessible. 1. Origin Disclosure The origin of primary materials or resources used in production must be declared. Examples may include: own cultivation or production local supplier sourcing regional sourcing imported materials Where applicable, geographic origin may be specified. 2. Material Transparency Primary materials used in the product must be declared. The declaration should provide visibility of: material categories natural or synthetic origin principal inputs used in production The objective is structural transparency of material composition. 3. Production Process Transparency The core production process must be described. The declaration should include: description of production stages responsible entity This ensures visibility and responsibility for production structure. Responsibility Declaration The producer publishes a public declaration confirming that the information disclosed reflects the actual production structure. Example declaration: “This product is declared under the Origin Eco™ Standard. Origin of materials, material composition, and production process transparency are publicly disclosed under producer responsibility.” Documentation Requirements Implementation typically requires: one origin disclosure sheet one material transparency sheet one production process description one responsibility declaration The information should remain publicly accessible. Structural Benefit The declaration framework transforms: implicit environmental claims into structurally documented environmental transparency. This strengthens: supply chain clarity customer trust regulatory defensibility environmental accountability. Closing Principle Environmental credibility begins with transparent origin.

title: Minimal Self-Declaration Framework
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Carbon Integrity™ Minimal Self-Declaration Framework This framework provides a simple method for applying the Carbon Integrity™ Standard through transparent disclosure of carbon-related operational information. It is designed for immediate use by small and medium-sized organizations. This framework is not a certification. It does not calculate emissions. It establishes structural transparency for carbon communication. Implementation Steps Step 1 — Define the Operational Boundary Clearly define what the carbon-related statement covers. Examples: Production site only Production and packaging Production, packaging, and transport Full operational footprint Other clearly defined scope If the boundary is unclear, the declaration is invalid. Step 2 — Disclose Energy Use Declare the primary energy source used in operations. Examples: Grid electricity Renewable energy Mixed energy sources Other defined source If known, the organization may also disclose approximate annual consumption or renewable share. If information is not measured, declare: “Energy data currently not measured.” Transparency is more important than precision. Step 3 — Disclose Transport Conditions Declare the main transport method used for distribution. Examples: Truck Rail Ship Air Mixed transport methods If approximate distribution distance is known, it may be disclosed. Unknown information must not be presented as verified data. Step 4 — Disclose Material Inputs Declare primary raw materials and packaging types used in production. Examples: main material categories packaging type recycled material share (if applicable) Absence of recycled material must not be concealed. Step 5 — Declare Information Source State how the disclosed information was obtained. Examples: utility bills supplier documentation direct operational measurement internal operational estimation Assumptions must be clearly declared. Step 6 — Responsibility Declaration A public responsibility statement must be issued. Example declaration: “This Carbon Integrity™ Minimal Self-Declaration is made under the Carbon Integrity™ Standard. The declaring entity accepts responsibility for the transparency and accuracy of the disclosed information.” The declaration should include: responsible person or organization declaration date public contact reference The declaration may be published: on a website in sustainability documentation in product information via QR code reference Documentation Requirements Implementation requires only: one operational boundary description one disclosure sheet covering energy, transport, and materials one public responsibility declaration No certification required. No external audit required under the minimal implementation level. Structural Value Carbon Integrity™ transforms: unclear carbon communication into structured transparency and accountability: This strengthens: credibility of sustainability communication protection against greenwashing risk supply chain transparency readiness for future carbon reporting requirements Closing Principle Responsible carbon communication begins with transparent disclosure.

title: Minimal Self-Declaration Framework
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Air Integrity™ Minimal Self-Declaration Framework This framework enables organizations to apply the Air Integrity™ Standard through simple and transparent disclosure of operational activities that may affect air conditions. It is designed to be usable by small workshops, farms, and service businesses as well as larger operational facilities. This framework: does not measure air quality does not certify emissions does not replace environmental regulation It establishes visible operational transparency . Implementation Steps Step 1 — Identify Air-Relevant Activities Review operational activities and determine whether any process may influence air conditions. Possible categories include: combustion processes (gas, diesel, biomass, oil) dust-generating operations (cutting, grinding, milling, dry material handling) solvent or chemical use (painting, coating, cleaning agents) fuel-based heating systems industrial processing with potential air emissions no emission-generating activity The applicable category must be publicly declared. If none apply, declare: “No active air emission-generating process.” Step 2 — Disclose Mitigation or Control Mechanisms Declare whether operational processes include mitigation systems. Examples include: no emission control systems natural ventilation mechanical ventilation filtration systems dust separation systems other mitigation mechanisms The framework requires disclosure of existing mechanisms rather than performance evaluation. Step 3 — Declare Measurement Status The organization must state the status of emission measurement. Possible declarations include: emissions regularly measured emissions occasionally measured emissions not measured measurement not legally required If measurement is not performed, this must be openly declared. Transparency is more important than technical completeness. Step 4 — Fuel Transparency (If Applicable) If combustion processes are used, declare: primary fuel type (gas, diesel, biomass, electricity, mixed sources) whether renewable energy sources are used (if applicable) No efficiency or emission calculation is required. Step 5 — Responsibility Declaration A public declaration confirming operational transparency must be issued. Example statement: “This Air Integrity™ Minimal Self-Declaration is made under the Air Integrity™ Standard. The declaring entity accepts responsibility for the transparency of the disclosed operational information.” The declaration should include: responsible person or organization declaration date public contact reference The declaration may be published: on a website within operational documentation on facility information sheets via QR code reference Documentation Requirements Implementation requires only: one operational disclosure sheet one description of air-relevant activities one public responsibility declaration No certification required. No external audit required under the minimal implementation level. Structural Value Air Integrity™ transforms: undisclosed operational reality into visible environmental transparency. This strengthens: trust with local communities operational awareness inside organizations environmental accountability credibility of environmental communication Closing Principle Operational honesty builds environmental trust.

title: Minimal Self-Declaration Framework
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Water Integrity™ Minimal Self-Declaration Framework Framework Type: Implementation Framework Related Standard: Water Integrity™ Standard Version: 1.0 Purpose This framework provides a minimal implementation model enabling producers to apply the Water Integrity™ Standard through transparent self-declaration. The framework establishes a simple disclosure structure allowing water use in production to be publicly documented. It does not replace regulatory obligations or certification systems. Implementation Principle The minimal level of Water Integrity™ implementation operates through producer self-declaration. Responsibility for accuracy and transparency remains with the declaring entity. The objective is to create visible water source and usage transparency within production systems. Minimal Implementation Model Water Integrity™ can be implemented through three core steps: Identify the water source Declare intended water use Declare water status and responsibility Completion of these steps establishes the minimal transparency baseline. Step 1 — Identify the Water Source The producer identifies and documents the water source category used in production. Possible categories include: municipal water supply private well surface water (river or lake) rainwater collection mixed sources If multiple sources are used, each source must be declared. Step 2 — Declare Intended Water Use The producer defines how water interacts with the production process. Typical usage categories include: irrigation washing produce ingredient inclusion processing use cleaning or sanitation The declared use should reflect the actual role of water in production. Step 3 — Declare Water Status The producer declares the known status of the water used in production. Examples of declared status include: municipal regulated potable water laboratory tested water (test date declared) private source with declared status non-potable operational water This framework does not impose laboratory testing requirements. It requires transparent declaration of the known status. Step 4 — Responsibility Declaration The producer publishes a short public statement acknowledging responsibility for the declared information. Example declaration: “This production declares water use under the Water Integrity™ Standard. Water source, intended use, and declared status are transparently disclosed under producer responsibility.” The declaration may be published: on a website in product documentation on supplier transparency sheets through QR code reference Documentation Requirements Minimal implementation requires: one water disclosure sheet one responsibility declaration public accessibility of the information No external certification or audit is required at the minimal implementation level. Structural Benefit The framework transforms: undocumented water inputs into declared water transparency. This strengthens: supply chain clarity customer trust inspection preparedness production accountability Implementation Characteristics The Water Integrity™ Minimal Self-Declaration Framework is: simple to apply tool-independent scalable suitable for small producers compatible with larger production systems It can be implemented immediately without infrastructure change. Closing Principle Transparent disclosure of water source and use establishes the minimal structural baseline for credible water-dependent production.

title: Minimal Self-Declaration Framework (WPPI-SD v1.0)
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Whole Process Plastic Integrity™ Minimal Self-Declaration Framework (WPPI-SD v1.0) Category: Environmental Integrity Standards Subcategory: Process & Material Integrity Status: Open Transparency Model Effective Date: 25 February 2026 This framework enables organizations to publicly declare Whole Process Plastic Integrity™ using a simple transparency model. It does not certify plastic-free status. It does not require laboratory testing. It establishes structured responsibility for plastic exposure disclosure across the operational process. Implementation Steps Step 1 — Define Process Boundary The declaring entity must define the operational scope of the declaration. Examples: single production facility multiple facilities production only production and packaging full chain including logistics Undefined process boundaries invalidate the declaration. Step 2 — Identify Plastic Exposure Points The entity reviews the production chain and identifies any plastic interaction points. Examples include: raw material packaging processing equipment contact auxiliary materials storage systems product packaging transport and handling systems If no intentional plastic components exist, this must be explicitly declared. Step 3 — Declare Plastic Integrity Tier The entity must select and declare one classification tier: Process Plastic Controlled (PPC) Plastic exposure minimized with declared control mechanisms. Process Plastic Minimal (PPM) Very limited plastic interaction within the process chain. Whole Process Plastic-Free (WPPF) No intentional plastic components present within the declared process boundary. Undeclared classification invalidates the claim. Step 4 — Contamination Awareness Statement The entity must acknowledge whether potential contamination pathways exist. Examples include: equipment abrasion transport exposure environmental contamination If no known contamination risks are identified, this must be declared. Step 5 — Responsibility Declaration A public declaration must be issued confirming responsibility for the disclosure. Example statement: “This Whole Process Plastic Integrity™ declaration is made under the WPPI™ Standard. The declaring entity accepts responsibility for the transparency and accuracy of the disclosed process information.” The declaration should include: legal entity name responsible person declaration date public contact reference The declaration may be published: on a website on product documentation in supply chain documentation via QR code reference Documentation Requirements Implementation requires only: a defined process boundary a list of identified plastic exposure points a selected integrity tier a public responsibility declaration No external certification required under the minimal self-declaration model. Structural Value WPPI™ Self-Declaration transforms: uncertain plastic claims into transparent process accountability. This supports: supply chain transparency contamination awareness credible plastic reduction claims future certification readiness. Closing Principle Plastic integrity is not determined by a label. It emerges from transparent control of the entire production process.

title: Minimal Self-Declaration Implementation Framework
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS — Master Index Asset Identity Standard Minimal Self-Declaration Implementation Framework Document Type: Implementation Framework Related Standard: Economic & Value Standards Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Version: 1.0 Date: 7 March 2026 1. Purpose This framework defines the minimum conditions required for an entity to declare implementation of the Asset Identity Standard. The framework allows organizations to adopt the standard through self- declaration without requiring formal certification. Self-declaration supports early adoption and transparent implementation of asset identity structures. 2. Declaration Principle An entity may publicly declare: “Asset Identity Standard Compatible System” only if the system implements the minimum identity conditions defined in this framework. The declaring entity remains responsible for the accuracy of the declaration. 3. Minimum Implementation Requirements To declare compatibility with the Asset Identity Standard, a system must implement the following elements. 3.1 Unique Asset Identity Each asset must possess a unique identity reference. The identity must allow the asset to be distinguished from all other assets within the system > 3.2 Origin Recording The system must record the origin of the asset. Origin may include: issuing authority creation event system admission event registration reference 3.3 Lifecycle Reference The system must allow the identity of the asset to be referenced during lifecycle events. Lifecycle events may include: validation activation transfer suspension state change 3.4 Responsibility Reference The system must define the entity responsible for maintaining the asset identity record. Responsibility may be assigned to: an organization a system authority environmental accountability a protocol governance mechanism 4. Transparency Organizations declaring compatibility should make available: identity structure description system boundaries lifecycle event structure This enables external observers to understand how asset identities operate within the system. 5. Optional Independent Verification Self-declaration does not require independent verification. However, organizations may voluntarily request: third-party verification internal audit review governance oversight 6. Declaration Statement Entities implementing the framework may publicly state: “This system implements the Asset Identity Standard through a self-declared identity framework.” Such declaration does not imply certification by OOF™. 7. Important Clarification Self-declaration: does not constitute certification does not imply endorsement by OOF™ represents a transparency statement by the implementing entity

title: Minimal Self-Declaration Implementation Framework
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS — Master Index Value Activation Standard (VAS) Minimal Self-Declaration Implementation Framework Document Type: Implementation Framework Related Standard: Value Activation Standard (VAS) Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Version: 1.0 Date: 7 March 2026 1. Purpose This document defines the minimum conditions required for an entity to publicly declare implementation of the Value Activation Standard (VAS). The framework allows organizations to adopt the standard without requiring formal certification. Self-declaration enables early adoption while preserving structural transparency. 2. Declaration Principle An entity may declare: “VAS Compatible Economic Activation Model” only if the system implements the minimum requirements defined in this framework. The declaring entity remains fully responsible for the accuracy of the declaration. 3. Minimum Implementation Requirements To declare compatibility with the Value Activation Standard , a system must implement the following components. 3.1 Asset Admission Layer The system must define how assets enter the economic environment. The admission process must: > record asset origin assign asset identity define the initial inactive state of the asset All newly admitted assets must begin in an inactive economic state. 3.2 Validation Layer The system must define validation rules before economic activation. Validation may include: origin verification compliance checks governance compatibility system integrity evaluation Assets failing validation must remain inactive. 3.3 Activation Rule The system must clearly define the conditions under which an asset transitions from inactive state to active value state. Activation conditions must be: deterministic documented traceable Activation events must be recorded. 3.4 Value Flow Definition The system must define how value flows after activation. The value flow model must specify: distribution mechanisms responsible entities governance rules Value flows must be observable within the system architecture. 3.5 Responsibility Anchor A responsible entity must be defined. The entity declaring implementation must: maintain system documentation ensure transparency of activation rules provide public explanation of the activation model 4. Transparency Requirement Entities declaring compatibility should publish: the activation logic validation criteria system boundaries This ensures that external observers can understand the value activation process. 5. Optional Independent Verification Independent verification is not required for self-declaration. However, organizations may voluntarily request: third-party verification internal audit review governance oversight 6. Declaration Statement Organizations implementing the framework may publicly state: “This system implements the Value Activation Standard (VAS) using a self-declared activation model.” Such declaration does not imply certification by OOF™. 7. Important Clarification Self-declaration under this framework: does not constitute certification does not imply endorsement by OOF™ represents a voluntary transparency statement by the implementing entity 8. Strategic Purpose The Self-Declaration Framework exists to encourage early adoption of the Value Activation Standard. By lowering implementation barriers, the framework allows systems to experiment with integrity-based economic activation models before formal governance structures are established.

title: Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF)
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS ArtData™ Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Standard Reference: ArtData™ Standard v1.0 Category: AI & Data Integrity Standards (AI) Purpose: Practical implementation guidance for datasets designated as ArtData™ Compliant 1. Implementation Principle ArtData™ implementation is based on a simple rule: If the origin, identity, history, and responsibility of a dataset are visible, the dataset becomes structurally accountable. The framework therefore focuses on minimum structural transparency , not complex technical infrastructure. 2. Minimum Implementation Steps To implement ArtData™ compliance, an organization must complete the following steps. Step 1 — Declare Dataset Origin The dataset origin must be documented. Minimum requirement: source category acquisition method Examples: internal data collection licensed dataset public dataset sensor-generated data research dataset The origin description must be stored in the dataset record. Step 2 — Assign Dataset Identity Anchor Each dataset must receive a unique structural identity. Minimum requirement: dataset identifier version number dataset hash or integrity reference Example: Dataset ID: ARTD-DS-00021 Version: 1.0 Integrity Hash: SHA256 reference This ensures dataset traceability across systems. Step 3 — Record Dataset Time Continuity The dataset lifecycle must be documented. Minimum requirement: creation date modification timestamps If the dataset changes, a new version record must be created. Step 4 — Document Dataset Transformations Any modification to the dataset must be recorded. Examples include: filtering annotation or labeling preprocessing formatting changes dataset merging Minimum documentation: transformation type date of modification responsible entity or system Step 5 — Declare Responsible Entity A legally identifiable entity must accept responsibility for the dataset. Minimum requirement: organization name responsible person or department public contact reference The responsible entity must confirm that dataset documentation is accurate. 3. ArtData™ Compliance Record Each ArtData™ dataset should maintain a simple dataset declaration record containing: Dataset ID Dataset version Source origin description Creation date Modification history Transformation documentation Responsible entity declaration This record may be stored: in dataset metadata in internal documentation in a dataset registry within a data governance system. 4. Public Responsibility Statement (Optional) Organizations may publish the following statement: “This dataset is maintained under ArtData™ structural integrity conditions. Dataset origin, identity, lifecycle history, and responsible entity information are documented in accordance with the ArtData™ Standard.” Public disclosure is optional but recommended. 5. Implementation Effort ArtData™ implementation requires minimal infrastructure. Typical implementation effort: documentation of dataset origin dataset identity assignment lifecycle record maintenance No external certification or mandatory audit is required under Version 1.0. 6. Structural Outcome When implemented correctly, ArtData™ provides: dataset traceability lifecycle transparency structural accountability improved AI training reproducibility reduced operational risk in AI systems ArtData™ establishes the minimum structural integrity foundation for AI datasets .

title: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property OOF® defines the structural conditions under which systems are valid, interoperable, and aligned with reality. What MIP® Is MIP® (Methodological Intellectual Property) is a framework for protecting methodologies, standards, and system structures. It protects: how systems are defined how meaning is structured how logic is connected how validation conditions are established MIP® does not protect ideas as content. It protects methodological structure and canonical meaning. Open and Protected by Design OOF® methodologies are: openly accessible freely usable globally available Open access allows: reading understanding implementation system usage Protection ensures: meaning is not altered structure is not redefined system logic is not fragmented Open use does not grant the right to alter structure or redefine meaning. Protection does not restrict use. It preserves integrity. What Is Open The following is open to all: access to methodologies use within systems implementation in practice learning and research No permission is required to use OOF® methodologies. What Is Protected The following must remain intact: canonical definitions structural design dependency logic validation conditions These elements cannot be modified without creating a non-canonical system state. Use and Validity Use of OOF® methodologies is free. Validity exists only when: canonical meaning is preserved structural integrity is maintained system dependencies remain intact A system may use OOF® methodologies freely. Only structurally aligned systems are considered valid. Reference and Origin A reference to the canonical source supports: traceability transparency system alignment For regulatory and interoperability purposes, systems must provide: a reference to the source a reference anchored in time A reference anchored in time establishes: origin priority traceability Without it, a system cannot be considered: auditable verifiable for use in regulated environments compatible within OOF® system interactions Global Methodological Protection MIP® operates as a globally applicable methodological protection framework. It defines protection at the level of: meaning structure system logic This protection is not limited to a single jurisdiction. It provides a globally consistent reference for methodological integrity, enabling: cross-border comparability regulatory interpretation system interoperability MIP® establishes methodologies as globally protected structural assets, independent of local legal implementation. Full Methodology Protection Scope MIP® ensures integrity across the full lifecycle of a methodology. This includes: meaning integrity structural integrity context integrity propagation integrity execution integrity validation integrity economic integrity Validation Signal OOF® defines three system states: Open Use Compatible Validated These states are: fixed non-interchangeable consistently applied across all systems No additional states exist within the OOF® system. Monetization Conditions Only valid methodologies may be monetized. A methodology cannot be monetized if: it lacks traceable origin it lacks defined identity it is not structurally aligned with OOF® conditions Monetization requires: traceable origin defined identity modular structure compatibility with the OOF® system No exceptions apply. Protection Scope MIP® protects: methodologies as structured systems standards as defined conditions of operation monetization logic as derived from validated system states interpretation integrity across human and AI environments MIP® ensures that: methodologies cannot be redefined standards cannot be structurally altered monetization cannot occur without valid system state AI cannot reinterpret meaning outside canonical definitions Context and Misuse Integrity Use of canonical definitions outside valid context may result in: semantic distortion misleading representation false system claims Such use is considered non-canonical within the OOF® system. Where misuse leads to: misrepresentation structural imitation misleading communication toward users or markets it may be evaluated by: independent entities authorized validation structures competent regulatory or judicial bodies System Enforcement Principle OOF® does not enforce. However: systems that violate canonical meaning or structure become non-valid systems without traceable origin cannot be verified systems outside defined conditions cannot be considered compatible Non-compliant systems may continue to exist, but they cannot participate in: validated environments interoperable systems auditable frameworks Final Statement MIP® protects methodologies, standards, monetization logic, and interpretation integrity across human and AI systems. In cases of misuse, competent regulatory, judicial, or authorized validation structures may act under applicable legal and regulatory frameworks. OOF® defines. Others may act.

title: MLM — Mutation Logging Module
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS MLM — Mutation Logging Module OriginID: OOF-OID-GOV-SESCS-MLM-2026-04-09-0001 Category: Governance & Enforcement Module: Mutation Logging Module (MLM) Type: Traceability & Audit Module Standard: Self-Evolving Systems Control Standard (SESCS) Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical Module Effective Date: 9 April 2026 Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Compatibility: SESCS · MTVF · TSA · EVIP · ArtData · AI Governance Systems · ORGS Canonical Definition System Mutation Logging Module (MLM) defines the mandatory recording, traceability, and audit structure for all system mutations occurring within self-evolving systems. Base Without mutation logging: system changes become invisible errors cannot be traced responsibility cannot be assigned audit is impossible A system that cannot explain its changes cannot be trusted. Protocol Any system capable of mutation MUST: record every mutation event store mutation data in immutable form assign timestamp and origin to each change ensure auditability of mutation history Absence of mutation logging results in: Non-Traceable System State (NTS) Scope MLM applies to: AI agents generating new logic systems modifying execution pathways autonomous optimization systems adaptive enterprise systems runtime mutation environments Methodology detect mutation event capture mutation data assign timestamp identify mutation origin store mutation record enable audit access Mutation Record Structure Each mutation MUST include: mutation identifier timestamp origin (human / system / hybrid) affected component description of change pre-state reference post-state reference Structural Rule (Critical) No mutation is valid unless it is recorded. Immutability Requirement Mutation logs MUST be: tamper-resistant append-only verifiable Deletion or alteration of logs is prohibited. MIF — Minimal Implementation Framework Step 1 — Mutation Detection Detect any system change. Minimum: mutation trigger captured Step 2 — Record Creation Create mutation record. Minimum: timestamp mutation identifier Step 3 — Origin Identification Assign origin. Minimum: human / system / hybrid Step 4 — Storage Store mutation log. Minimum: persistent storage non-editable format MIF+ — Extended Implementation Framework Includes all MIF requirements plus: cryptographic log verification distributed logging systems real-time logging streams cross-system log synchronization integration with TSA classification anomaly detection in mutation logs Decision Logic Mutation state is: TRACEABLE → recorded and verifiable NON-TRACEABLE → missing or incomplete logging Use Case 1 — AI System Behavior Change Scenario AI system modifies its decision logic. Problem change is not recorded behavior becomes unpredictable no traceability Application MLM enforces: full mutation logging timestamped change tracking Result system behavior is traceable changes can be audited trust is maintained Use Case 2 — System Failure Investigation Scenario System produces incorrect or harmful output. Problem no record of system changes failure source cannot be identified Application MLM provides: full mutation history traceable change sequence Result root cause identified responsibility assigned system corrected Compatibility MLM operates with: MCM — defines mutation boundaries MVM — validates mutations RAM — assigns responsibility RIM — enables rollback TSA — classifies trust MTVF — validation layer Structural Principle If a system changes, the change must be recorded. Closing Statement Unrecorded change is invisible risk. Invisible risk cannot be controlled. Mutation Logging Module (MLM) establishes a non-negotiable condition: Every mutation must be recorded, traceable, and auditable. Related Documents → SESCS Standard → SESCS — Master Index

title: Modular Architecture™
text: Modular Architecture™ Modular Family Principle for Governance Intelligence Engine™ A fundamental principle of Governance Intelligence Engine™ is modularity through governance families. Governance Intelligence Engine™ is designed as a family-based governance architecture rather than a module-based architecture. Individual governance families may operate independently or in combination with other governance families. However, when a governance family is selected, its internal methodological integrity should remain preserved wherever compatibility, auditability, reproducibility, governance validity, and methodological consistency are required. The objective is not forcing organizations to utilize the entire Governance Intelligence Engine™. The objective is enabling organizations, institutions, AI systems, robotics platforms, autonomous agents, military environments, and future governance ecosystems to utilize the governance capabilities required for their specific conditions while preserving methodological integrity when compatibility is desired. Governance Family Architecture Governance Intelligence Engine™ is composed of governance families. Each family represents a complete governance capability rather than an isolated analytical step. Families may operate independently or in combination. Semantic Governance™ Provides semantic understanding, canonical definitions, categorization, governance meaning, and architectural space identification. Core Question: What is it? Governance Navigation™ Provides structured problem discovery, localization, mapping, dependency analysis, propagation analysis, and governance diagnostics. Core Question: Where is the problem? Governance Simulation™ Provides scenario evaluation, future-state analysis, risk simulation, dependency impact analysis, escalation evaluation, and governance re-simulation. Core Question: What could happen? Governance Architecture On Demand™ Provides governance architecture generation based on identified governance conditions and analytical findings. Core Question: What should be built? Operational Reality™ Provides reality validation through observation of actual implementation outcomes. Core Question: What actually happened? ART™ Provides Audit in Real Time™ capabilities for continuous evidence collection and validation. Core Question: What can be verified? ArtData® Provides validated governance evidence generated through Operational Reality™ and ART™. Core Question: What evidence remains? Governance Intelligence Lifecycle Semantic Governance™ ↓ Governance Navigation™ ↓ Governance Simulation™ ↓ Governance Architecture On Demand™ ↓ Operational Reality™ ↓ ART™ ↓ ArtData® The lifecycle provides an architectural pathway from meaning to evidence. It enables humans, organizations, AI systems, robotics platforms, autonomous agents, and future self-healing systems to move from problem understanding toward validated operational evidence. AI, Robotics, and Autonomous Agent Logic Governance Intelligence Engine™ may serve as AI-readable governance logic for future autonomous systems. Its governance families can guide AI systems, robotics environments, autonomous agents, and self-healing systems in how to: identify problems, classify problems, localize problems, evaluate dependencies, simulate possible outcomes, design governance responses, evaluate corrective actions, preserve audit trails, validate outcomes, generate evidence. The objective is not merely intelligent action. The objective is governable, auditable, explainable, and traceable action. A self-healing agent should not merely repair itself. It should be able to demonstrate how the problem was identified, where it was localized, which risks were simulated, why a corrective action was selected, and which evidence validates the outcome. Independent Module Use Governance Intelligence Engine™ recommends the use of complete governance families whenever methodological integrity, auditability, compatibility, reproducibility, and governance validity are required. However, individual modules may also be used independently when an organization requires only a specific governance capability. Examples include: Problem Localization™ only, Risk Simulation™ only, Governance Re-Simulation™ only, Validation Layer Design™ only, ArtData® only. Such usage may be appropriate within organizations, institutions, security environments, military structures, robotics platforms, autonomous systems, research environments, or implementation-specific governance architectures. However, when individual modules are used outside their complete governance family, responsibility for implementation, integration, compatibility, validation, and operational performance remains with the adopting organization. OOF® provides the architectural logic. The implementing party determines how that logic is operationalized within its environment. Compatibility Principle Complete governance families preserve compatibility with the broader Governance Intelligence Engine™ ecosystem. Individual modules may remain useful independently, but they may not provide the same level of methodological continuity, auditability, reproducibility, governance validity, or ecosystem compatibility unless integrated according to the broader architecture. The principle is simple: Governance families preserve compatibility. Individual modules provide selective capability. Implementation determines operational validity. Example Applications Governance Diagnostics Engagement Uses: Semantic Governance™ Governance Navigation™ Output: Governance Intelligence Report™ Strategic Governance Assessment Uses: Semantic Governance™ Governance Navigation™ Governance Simulation™ Output: Governance Intelligence Report™ Governance Architecture Design Uses: Semantic Governance™ Governance Navigation™ Governance Simulation™ Governance Architecture On Demand™ Output: Governance Architecture Recommendation™ Self-Healing AI Agent Uses: Governance Navigation™ Governance Simulation™ Governance Re-Simulation™ Operational Reality™ Output: Auditable corrective-action pathways. Auditable Autonomous Agent Uses: Governance Navigation™ Governance Simulation™ Operational Reality™ ART™ ArtData® Output: Auditable operational behavior and validated evidence trails. Selective Module Implementation Uses: selected modules only. Output: Implementation-specific governance capability. title: Module 1 — Identity Anchor
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Module 1 — Identity Anchor Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Identity Module: Identity Anchor Type: Identity Module Standard: OBIDENITY™ — Origin-Bound Identity Standard Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 19 March 2026 Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Founder & System Design Architect: Miroslav Pis Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Identity Anchor defines the structural conditions under which an identity is created as a unique, non-replicable origin point bound to a verifiable origin event. The Identity Anchor establishes the existence of identity and serves as the immutable reference for its entire lifecycle. Why This Matters Without a defined origin, identity cannot be distinguished from duplication or imitation. Most identity systems allow: duplication reassignment overwrite loss of origin This creates environments where identity cannot be trusted. Identity Anchor ensures that identity begins as a single, verifiable event that cannot be replicated or replaced. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Create Unique Identity Anchor Identity must be created as a unique, non-reusable anchor. Minimum requirement: unique identity anchor no duplication no reuse of identity Step 2 — Bind to Origin Event Identity must be linked to a verifiable origin. Minimum requirement: defined origin event recorded timestamp identifiable responsible entity Step 3 — Ensure Non-Overwriteability Identity Anchor must not be replaceable. Minimum requirement: no overwrite no reassignment no substitution Step 4 — Enable Anchor Verification The origin of identity must be verifiable. Minimum requirement: traceable origin record reconstructable creation event verifiable link to issuer Use Case 1 — Cross-Platform Identity Ownership Scenario An individual or entity operates across multiple platforms, each creating separate identities. Application Identity Anchor establishes a single origin-bound identity independent of platforms. Result identity is no longer controlled by platforms identity persists across systems no duplication or fragmentation of identity Use Case 2 — AI-Driven Identity Representation Scenario A public figure or organization uses AI agents to represent their identity in communication and interaction. Application Identity Anchor binds all representations to a verifiable origin identity. Result AI interactions remain tied to a real identity impersonation becomes detectable trust is preserved across digital interactions Structural Principle Identity begins only once. Without a verifiable beginning, identity does not exist. Closing Statement An identity without origin is not an identity. Related Documents → OBIDENITY™ Standard

title: Module 2 — Identity Continuity
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Module 2 — Identity Continuity Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Identity Module: Identity Continuity Type: Identity Module Standard: OBIDENITY™ — Origin-Bound Identity Standard Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 19 March 2026 Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Founder & System Design Architect: Miroslav Pis Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Identity Continuity defines the structural conditions under which an identity persists over time without loss, fragmentation, or replacement. Continuity exists only when identity is maintained through a traceable, append-only sequence of events that preserves its link to the original identity anchor. Why This Matters An identity that cannot persist over time loses its meaning. Without identity continuity: identity may be fragmented across systems identity history may be lost identity may be replaced without detection identity may exist only as a temporary state This creates environments where identity cannot be reliably tracked or trusted. Identity Continuity ensures that identity is not only created, but also preserved as a continuous and traceable entity. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Maintain Append-Only Lifecycle Identity must evolve through an append-only event structure. Minimum requirement: no deletion of identity history no overwrite of past states continuous event recording Step 2 — Preserve Anchor Link All identity states must remain linked to the original Identity Anchor. Minimum requirement: no detachment from origin no creation of parallel identity chains no reassignment of identity lineage Step 3 — Prevent Fragmentation Identity must not split into multiple independent versions. Minimum requirement: single continuous identity chain no duplicated identity branches no hidden identity forks Step 4 — Enable State Reconstruction Identity must be reconstructable at any point in time. Minimum requirement: full event history traceable timeline verifiable state at any moment Use Case 1 — Long-Term Digital Identity Persistence Scenario An individual uses multiple systems and platforms over time, with identities changing, merging, or disappearing. Application Identity Continuity ensures that identity remains consistent and traceable across all systems and time periods. Result identity persists beyond platforms full identity history remains intact no loss or fragmentation of identity over time Use Case 2 — Identity Evolution in AI Systems Scenario An AI agent evolves over time through updates, training, and interaction. Application Identity Continuity ensures that all changes remain linked to the original identity anchor and are traceable. Result clear lineage of AI identity traceable evolution of behavior and decisions no hidden replacement or reset of identity Structural Principle An identity that cannot be traced through time cannot be considered the same identity. Closing Statement Identity does not exist only at creation. It exists only if it continues. Related Documents → OBIDENITY™ Standard

title: Module 3 — Chain of Control
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Module 3 — Chain of Control Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Identity Module: Chain of Control Type: Identity Module Standard: OBIDENITY™ — Origin-Bound Identity Standard Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 19 March 2026 Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Founder & System Design Architect: Miroslav Pis Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Chain of Control defines the structural conditions under which control, authority, and responsibility over an identity remain continuous, traceable, and non- transferable without record. Integrity exists only when every action affecting identity can be linked to a responsible actor within a continuous chain of control. Why This Matters An identity without defined control cannot be governed. Without a chain of control: identity actions may have no accountable actor authority may be transferred without trace responsibility may become fragmented identity may be manipulated without detection This creates systems where identity exists, but responsibility does not. Chain of Control ensures that identity is always linked to accountable authority. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Define Control Authority Identity must have a defined controlling authority. Minimum requirement: identifiable controlling entity defined authority scope clear ownership or control reference Step 2 — Trace All Control Actions All actions affecting identity must be traceable. Minimum requirement: identifiable actor for each action recorded control events time-linked action history Step 3 — Preserve Control Continuity Control must remain continuous across time. Minimum requirement: no gaps in control chain no undefined transitions no anonymous authority changes Step 4 — Prevent Untraceable Transfer Control must not be transferred without record. Minimum requirement: traceable control transfer no hidden delegation no loss of accountability Use Case 1 — Identity Ownership and Transfer Scenario An identity is transferred between individuals, organizations, or systems. Application Chain of Control ensures that each transfer is recorded and traceable, preserving responsibility. Result clear ownership history traceable authority transitions no loss of accountability Use Case 2 — AI Agent Control and Governance Scenario An AI agent operates under changing control, such as different operators or governing entities. Application Chain of Control ensures that all control actions and authority changes are recorded and linked to responsible actors. Result traceable governance of AI identity clear accountability for actions reduced risk of uncontrolled identity manipulation Structural Principle Control without traceability is not control. Responsibility without continuity does not exist. Closing Statement An identity without accountable control is not governable. Related Documents → OBIDENITY™ Standard

title: Module 4 — Identity Integrity
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Module 4 — Identity Integrity Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Identity Module: Identity Integrity Type: Identity Module Standard: OBIDENITY™ — Origin-Bound Identity Standard Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 19 March 2026 Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Founder & System Design Architect: Miroslav Pis Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Identity Integrity defines the structural conditions under which an identity remains protected against replication, impersonation, unauthorized modification, or structural compromise. Integrity exists only when identity cannot be altered, duplicated, or simulated without detection. Why This Matters Even when identity has a valid origin and continuity, it can still be compromised. Without identity integrity: identity may be cloned or duplicated identity may be impersonated identity attributes may be altered unauthorized actions may go undetected This creates systems where identity exists but cannot be trusted. Identity Integrity ensures that identity remains authentic and resistant to manipulation. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Prevent Identity Replication Identity must not be duplicable. Minimum requirement: no creation of identical identity anchors no reuse of identity structure no parallel identity copies Step 2 — Detect Unauthorized Modification Changes to identity must be controlled and detectable. Minimum requirement: no silent modification traceable identity changes detection of unauthorized updates Step 3 — Protect Against Impersonation Identity must not be usable by unauthorized actors. Minimum requirement: verifiable control linkage no anonymous identity usage no identity simulation without detection Step 4 — Maintain Structural Integrity Identity structure must remain intact across its lifecycle. Minimum requirement: no hidden structural changes no corruption of identity data preservation of identity consistency Use Case 1 — Protection Against Identity Cloning Scenario An identity is copied or recreated to impersonate a real entity. Application Identity Integrity ensures that any duplication or unauthorized replication is detectable. Result prevention of identity cloning detection of duplicate identities preservation of identity authenticity Use Case 2 — Secure AI Identity Representation Scenario AI systems represent individuals, organizations, or agents in communication and decision-making. Application Identity Integrity ensures that only authorized representations are linked to the identity and that impersonation is detectable. Result trusted AI identity representation prevention of unauthorized impersonation secure interaction with identity-based systems Structural Principle An identity that can be copied or altered without detection cannot be trusted. Closing Statement Integrity protects identity from becoming imitation. Related Documents → OBIDENITY™ Standard

title: Module 5 — Identity State
text: OOF™ Core Methodology OS Module 5 — Identity State Category: Governance & Enforcement Subcategory: Identity Module: Identity State Type: Identity Module Standard: OBIDENITY™ — Origin-Bound Identity Standard Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Standard Effective Date: 19 March 2026 Authority: OOF™ Origin Open Foundation™ Founder & System Design Architect: Miroslav Pis Protection: MIP™ — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Identity State defines the structural conditions under which the current status of an identity can be determined, classified, and verified at any point in time. An identity is valid only when its state is observable, traceable, and derived from its full event history. Why This Matters An identity may exist, but without a defined state, it cannot be evaluated. Without identity state: identity status may be unclear compromised identities may remain undetected systems cannot distinguish valid from invalid identity decisions may rely on unknown identity conditions This creates environments where identity cannot be reliably used. Identity State ensures that identity is always measurable and interpretable. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Define Identity States The system must define observable identity states. Minimum requirement: valid compromised suspended restored unknown Step 2 — Link State to Event History Identity state must be derived from traceable events. Minimum requirement: state based on recorded events no arbitrary or hidden state assignment traceable logic for state changes Step 3 — Enable State Verification Identity state must be independently verifiable. Minimum requirement: reconstructable state from event history observable current state verifiable state transitions Step 4 — Maintain State Consistency Identity state must remain consistent with actual identity condition. Minimum requirement: no mismatch between state and reality no hidden state manipulation no undefined state changes Use Case 1 — Identity Trust Classification Scenario A system must determine whether an identity can be trusted for interaction, transaction, or decision-making. Application Identity State provides a clear classification of identity status based on its history and integrity. Result clear trust evaluation ability to filter valid vs compromised identities improved decision reliability Use Case 2 — Identity Recovery and Restoration Scenario An identity becomes compromised and requires restoration. Application Identity State tracks the transition from compromised to restored through verifiable events. Result traceable recovery process clear state transition history restored trust based on evidence Structural Principle An identity that cannot express its state cannot be evaluated. Closing Statement Identity is not only what it is. It is also the state it is in. Related Documents → OBIDENITY™ Standard

title: MPIM — Movement Prediction Interpretation Module
text: MPIM — Movement Prediction Interpretation Module Parent Standard: Physical Reality Interpretation Layer (PRIL™) Category: AI & Interpretation Subcategory: Movement Prediction Interpretation Type: Physical Interpretation Module Version: 1.0 Status: Canonical · Open Module Effective Date: 8 May 2026 Compatibility: OOF® Methodology OS™ · PRIL™ · CLIA® · RIS · INTEGROS® · SIMULOS® Authority: OOF® Protection: MIP® — Methodological Intellectual Property Canonical Language: English (UCL™) Canonical Definition Movement Prediction Interpretation Module defines the methodological conditions under which autonomous systems interpret and predict the movement of humans, vehicles, robots, objects, or dynamic environmental elements before generating physical action or embodied response. A system satisfies MPIM only if: movement is interpreted before physical execution predicted trajectories are evaluated under defined conditions dynamic change is treated as an operational interpretation problem uncertainty in movement prediction is recognized as an execution restriction condition physical action is limited when movement prediction interpretation is insufficient A system that detects movement without governed prediction interpretation does not satisfy MPIM. Module Function MPIM defines the dynamic movement interpretation layer of physical execution. It ensures that systems do not treat observed motion as sufficient for safe execution unless that motion is interpreted as future operational consequence. The module applies wherever systems must act in environments where nearby movement, directional change, acceleration, crossing, convergence, or trajectory uncertainty affect execution validity. Minimum Implementation Framework (MIF) Step 1 — Define Relevant Movement Context The organization must define what movement conditions are operationally relevant. Minimum requirement: relevant moving entities are identifiable movement context is explicit undefined dynamic behavior is excluded from valid execution logic Step 2 — Define Movement Interpretation Conditions The system must define how movement is interpreted. Minimum requirement: movement is not treated as raw signal only direction, speed, approach, and change conditions are explicitly interpreted uncertain movement recognition is not silently treated as valid certainty Step 3 — Define Prediction Logic The system must define how future movement paths are interpreted before execution. Minimum requirement: predicted trajectory logic is explicit crossing, convergence, and unstable path behavior are distinguishable prediction assumptions are not hidden Step 4 — Define Uncertainty and Restriction Conditions The system must define when uncertainty in movement prediction slows, stops, restricts, or escalates execution. Minimum requirement: uncertainty handling is explicit degraded trajectory confidence can restrict action continued physical action under uncertain movement conditions is not treated as valid Step 5 — Preserve Safety Over Motion Assumption The system must preserve safety above speed, completion pressure, or optimistic motion prediction. Minimum requirement: uncertain future movement overrides execution convenience predicted stability does not justify risk without bounded interpretation physical action remains subordinate to valid movement prediction conditions Step 6 — Restrict Invalid Execution The system must not be treated as valid if physical execution proceeds while movement prediction interpretation is absent, degraded, or unreliable. Minimum requirement: invalid execution conditions are identifiable degraded movement prediction blocks valid reliance motion sensing alone does not restore prediction validity Use Case 1 — Autonomous Vehicle or Mobile Robot Scenario An autonomous vehicle or mobile robot operates in an environment where humans, other vehicles, or moving objects may cross, converge, or change direction unexpectedly. Application MPIM is used to ensure: relevant movement conditions are defined dynamic trajectories are interpreted before execution uncertain path prediction restricts action movement-related execution remains governed by prediction validity Result The organization gains a stronger basis for preventing physical action from continuing when motion is sensed but future movement is not sufficiently interpreted. Use Case 2 — Industrial or Embodied Multi-Motion Environment Scenario A system operates in a space where robotic arms, transported items, humans, and machines move simultaneously, creating constantly changing dynamic conditions. Application MPIM is used to ensure: movement pathways are interpreted under defined logic convergence and crossing risks are recognized unstable motion prediction can slow, stop, or escalate execution physical action is bounded by dynamic interpretation conditions Result The organization gains a structurally governed movement-prediction layer instead of relying on visible motion alone as if it were enough for safe execution. Canonical Closing Statement If movement is not interpreted as future operational risk before action, physical execution is not structurally safe. Related Documents → Physical Reality Interpretation Layer (PRIL™)
